Comments on Annotation:
The book, The Surnames of Scotland, Their Origin, Meaning and History by George F. Black,
Ph.D., 1996, Eleventh Reprinting, The New York Public Library, New York, has been used
extensively in the regrouping of some surnames and adding information on the origin of
surnames and an example of an early record of a surname. ALL ANNOTATION ENTRIES IN
QUOTATION MARKS ARE QUOTATIONS FROM BLACK. Annotation is only partially
completed.

Editor’s Notes:
To facilitate searching for different spellings of the same surname, some regrouping of variants
of the same surname has been done from the original publications.
The Surnames of Scotland, by George F. Black, 1996, has been used as the authority for placing
variants of the same surname in closer proximity to each other.
The surname groupings from the four volumes have been placed together, usually in
chronological order. For example, Adamson 1583 - 1666, Adamson 1666 -1700, etc. The first
entry for each ent ry group is highlighted, but subsequent entries use a double comma (,,) for the
surname, followed by the first name. For example, Adamson, Alexr., B. and G.,
second s. of umq. Wm. A. 5 July 1524; „ Alexr., B. and G., second s. of umq. John A. 5 July
1524, etc.
Be inovative in the search parameters you use. For example, the spelling of the son’s and father’s
surnames may differ slightly. A wife’s given name is listed, but not her surname, while her
father’s given name may be abbreviated (e.g., Alexr.) and the surname given in full. Learn and
use variant spellings. Black is probably the best source.
Caution: Some names are inappropriately grouped under the same surname by the original
editors, probably due to poor penmanship, erasures and improper spelling. Know your
surname variants!

                             INTRODUCTION 1406 - 1700.
THE Register of Burgesses and Guild-Brethren of the City of Edinburgh is contained in a
number of MS. volumes, carefully preserved in the Town Clerk’s fire-proof safe in the City
Chambers.
After 30th May 1666 the entries of apprentices are contained in the scroll volumes, along with
those of burgesses and guild-brethren. The roll of these is being issued separately.
Of these volumes Nos. 1 to 8 have been used in compiling the roll which follows, beginning at
17th May 1487, and ending in Vol. 8 at 31st December 1700.
The very early entries are taken from the minutes or records of the Town Council.
The scroll volumes, whose contents have not been entered in the official volumes, or have been
lost with them, are very badly and hastily written, and in many cases the names, Christian and,
more particularly, family, are very difficult to decipher, the rather that no rule of spelling has
been observed, and the attempts at a phonetic rendering are bewildering. The Celtic names are
really dreadful.
The earliest entries, being in ancient script, and also in Latin abounding in contractions, offered
obstacles which would, it is to be feared, have wrecked the undertaking, but for the help, so
graciously given, chiefly by Mr. John Jarvis, Session-Clerk of the City Churches, by Mr. Henry
M. Paton of H.M. Register House, and by Miss Marguerite Wood, Keeper of the Burgh Records,
to all of whom I tender my very grateful thanks.

CHARLES B. BOOG WATSON.
NOTES ON THE GUILD REGISTER, EXPLANATIONS, GLOSSARY, ETC 1406 - 1700.

GUILD REGISTER.
Vol.1. Size 11 in. x 7 in. Marked 24 May 1487 to 8 Jan. 1579, but the first entry is 17 May 1487,
the last 12 Feb. 1579-80. (It must be remembered that under the “old style” the year began on the
25th March.) The folios, as indicated by pencil notes at the beginning of the volume, are badly
arranged. This must be noted in making search for entries.
There is a blank between Jan. 1500-1 and 30 March 1508 ; also between 24 May 1509 and 27
Sept. 1520.
The folios are numbered. The earlier entries are in Latin. (See 15 March 1560-1.) The volume
closes with “latin letters”
Vol. 2. Size 11 in. x 7 in. The folios are not numbered. It begins with several “Acts,” and
contains entries of burgesses and guild-brethren from 13 April 1580 to 25 Dec. 1616.
Vol. 3. 11½ in. x 7½ in. The folios are not numbered. It contains entries from 1 Jan. 1617-18 to
18 Feb. 1669-70. A massive volume, bound in wooden boards, covered with leather, having
brass corners and studs, with two brass- hinged bands, formerly fitted with hasps suiting the two
locks for which two keys were required.
On the fly leaf is written : “The lokkit guild buik of the burgh of Edinburgh, Maid be David
Aikenheid, deyne of gild (And afterwards more than once provost.) of the said burgh, the fourt
year of his office. Conteyning all the burgesses and gild brother admittit and resavit efter this
present day the first day of Januar one thousand six hundrethe and sevinteene years.”
It is beautifully written.
Vol. 4. Size 7½ in. x 5½ in. The folios are not numbered. It begins with the prayer to be used at
the meeting of the court, the oaths to be taken by burgesses and gildbrethren respectively, and the
scale of fees for booking of ‘prentices, and admission of burgesses and guild-brethren ; then
entries from 24 Feb. 1669-70 to Dec. 1676, and at the end jottings of fees paid.
Vol. 5. Size 8 7/8 in. x 6½ in. The folios are not numbered. It begins with the form of prayer, and
the oaths to be taken ; then entries from 3 Jan. 1677 to 13 Sept. 1691, and at the end jottings of
fees paid.
Vol. 6. Size 7¼ in. x 5¾ in. The folios are not numbered. It begins with the form of prayer, then
entries from 10 Oct. 1691 to 14 April 1697, and ends with jottings of fees paid.
Vol. 7. Size 12½ in. x 8 in. The folios are not numbered. It contains entries from 5 Jan. 1687 to
12 March 1695 and is beautifully written, but less than half the volume has been written up ; the
remainder is blank.
Vol. 8. Size 7¾ in. x 6 in. The folios are not numbered. It contains entries from 21 April 1697 to
4 June 1703, beginning with four pages of entries of loans from the guild funds, and jottings at
the end of fees paid.
Vols. 4, 5, 6 and 8 are evidently scroll entries of burgesses, guild-brethren and ‘prentices. These
have been only partly written up in the court books. Vols. 1, 2, 3 and 7, which are very carefully
written, contain no entries of ‘prentice bookings.
NAMES [1761 - 1841].
It is rare in the earlier records to find any one entering as apprentice or burgess burdened with
more than the two names, Christian and surname, but these begin to appear early in the
eighteenth century, e.g. John Hall Young, 29 April 1729. Towards the end of that century they
increase in frequency.
Matthew is always spelled Mathew. Occasional changes occur between father and son : James
Hog Dixon, son of James Dickson, entered prentice to George Hardie, tertius, baker, 9/12/1779.


ADDRESSES [1761 - 1841].
In most cases none, only trade or occupation.
Note.— It is always “ Canongate” or “ Cowgate,” without the the.
Some very vague :—Alexander Matheson, carter, near Edinburgh.
Robert Ponton, in the Town of Dalmainy, nigh Cramond.
The “ Water of Leith.” That is the Village of the Water of Leith, where the Town’s eleven mills
stood on the south side of the water, opposite the Dean Village on the north side.
9 Feb, 1786.—John Brough, wright in the “New Town.”
7 Apr. 1787.—Patrick Taylor, painter in the “ New Town.”
14 Aug. 1787.—John Clark, mason in the Extended Royalty.
26 Sept. 1787.—Alexr. Preston, residenter at the Castle of clouts.
5 Dec. 1793.—Charles Fraser, manufacturer on Leith Walk.
12 May 1794-—John Black, baker in Nicolson’s Street.
INTRODUCTION, 1701 - 1760.
In this volume is continued the Roll or Register of Burgesses and Guild-brethren of the City of
Edinburgh from 1st January 1701 to 31st December 1760. Illustrative notes, glossary, etc., will
be found at the end of the volume.

CHARLES B. BOOG WATSON.

INTRODUCTION [1761 - 1841].
In this volume is contained the Roll or Register of Burgesses and Guild-brethren of the City of
Edinburgh from 1st January 1761 to 31st December 1841.
Some notes, etc., will be found at the beginning and end of the volume.

CHARLES B. BOOG WATSON.

NOTE [1761 - 1841].
Between the end of April and 11 May 1797 no days of the month are given, only the month. The
entries during that period are given as—May 1797.

- A-

The origin of this surname in Scotland is unclear. "It is probable that in some instances this name
is a shortened translation of MacNab, which in Gaelic means 'son of the abbot' . . . " In England
and Ireland the name is a diminutive for Abraham, "... but I have found no instance of such use
in Scotland." An early record is "Alexander Abbot is in record as witness in Glasgow c. 1290 ...
Abbot, Andw., B., by mandate of the provost, Dominus Thos. Tod, 31 Dec. 1494-2 Mar. 1498-9

Variants of the surname Abel. Derived from "... a not uncommon personal name in the Middle
Ages, derived from the Biblical Abel, Hebrew Hebhel, a name of uncertain meaning, but usually
interpreted 'breath.' "An early record is "Master Abell, clericus regis, was one of the members of
a mission sent to England to ask restoration of the earldom of Huntingdon in 1237 ... "
Abell (Able, Eball), Alexr., B., glassinwryt (musket), as p. to Johne Fockhart, glassinwryt, B.
  24 July 1633
„ James, B., tayleor, by act of C. of 18 July 15 Aug. 1694

Variants of the surname Abercrombie. "Of Territorial origin from the barony, now parish of the
same name in Fife." An early record is "William de Abercromby of the county of Fife did
homage in 1296."

Variants of the surname Abernethy. " 'The origin of the Abernethies,' says the late Sir James
Balfour Paul, 'cannot be stated with any certainty.' In the twelfth century they appear to have
occupied the position of lay abbots of the Culdee Monastery of Abernethy in Strathearn. This
would seem to show that they were descended from original native stock and not of Saxon or
Norman origin." "The first of the Abernethies on record is Hugh, who appears to have died about
the middle of the twelfth century."

Black provides a somewhat lengthy review of various proposed origins for the surname Adair,
but concludes with " 'As a matter of fact... the name is ... simply a form of Edgar, [the]
progenitor being probably Edgar, son of Duvenald, a leader at the battle of the Standard,
grandson of Donegal of Morton Castle, a descendant of whom, Robert [sic, Thomas] Edzear had
a charter from Robert Bruce of the lands of Kildonan, adjacent to which are those of Kinhilt. In
confirmation of this we also find the name of Edgar attaching to a hill on his property at
Dromore' ... In a footnote Agnew adds: 'In the Lochnaw charter chest various deeds prove the
name Edzear and Adair to have been interchangeable with the Gallo way Adairs. In a Charter
dated 1625 the name is spelled in both forms on the same page.' "

Adam was a very popular name for boys in both England and Scotland and it is presumed the
name has many origins. Black debunks the theory that " 'all the Adams, Macadams, Adamsons,
and Adies in Scotland are descended ... from Duncan Adam, who lived in the reign of Robert the
Bruce, ..." Two early records are "Adam, sub-prior of Melrose became abbot of Cupar, 1189 ...
Adam son of Adam was one of the witnesses to the charter by William Bruce to Adam of
Carlyle of the lands of Kynemund, c. [about] 1194-1214 ..." Also, see Addison, which is "...
from the diminutive of Adam, and is therefore the same as Adamson."

early records are "Adam Reid, familiar servitor of king Kames IV is referred to in 1513 As Ade
Rede. William Ade of Inverkeithing rendered homage in 1296 ..."

Aikin. See Aitken
"No satisfactory explanation of this name is known. Lower suggested that it was a modification
of OE. [Old English] Agemund, Ferguson and Harrison derive it from OE. Æcemann, 'oakman'
(æc+mann), Sir Herbert Maxwell ... finds its origin in OE. ace manne, 'an infirm person,' and
Dr. Henry Bradley suggested that the first element is perhaps ac, and tha t the name may possibly
represent an OE. acumann, which became Acemann by later development, but a form Acemann
is not known. The story told of the officer who had command of the troops besieging
Macbeth in Dunsinane Castle ordering his men to march to the attack with branches of oak taken
brom Birnam Wood, and on that account obtained the name of Aikman, is still an article of faith
with some." An early record is "Alisaundre Akeman of Lanarkshire who rendered homage in
1296 ... is believed to be the first of the name recorded in Scotland."

Air. See Aird.
Caution! Air/Ayr and Aird are two distinct surnames according to Black. They may have been
grouped below. Black does not specifically say it, but it appears he believes there were at least
two origins for Air, although he is vague about the first origin. (1) Perhaps "The lands of
William Ayr or Air in the lordship of Dunbar are mentioned in 1522 ... (2) Of local origin from
the royal burgh of Ayr." An early record of the latter is "Reginald of Ayr was clerk in Ayr, 1287
Aird is "Of local origin from a place of the name. It may be from Aird near Hurlford, Ayrshire,
or from the hamlet of Aird in the parish of Inch, Wigtownshire, more probably from the former."
An early record of Aird is "Nicoll Ard and William Ard, followers of the earl of Cassilis, were
respited for murder in 1526 ..."

Variants of the surname Acheson. Acheson, Aicheson, Aitcheson, Aitchison and Atkinson "... all
mean 'son of Adam,' the first four from the diminutive Atty, and the last from the diminutive
Adkin with the d sharpened to t." An early record is "Johannes filius [son of] Ade [Adam],
custumar of North Berwick in 1384, appears in 1387 as John Atkynsoun, and in following years
again as Johannes filius Ade ..."

Variants of the surname Aiken. Aiken, Aitken, Aitkin Aitkins, Atkin, Atkins "... are double
diminutives of Adam, formed from Ad the diminutive of Adam with the diminutive suffix -kin
(OE. [Old English] -cen), and with the d sharpened to t.
These names have been also explained as = little Atty or Arthur, but the preceding origin is the
more likely one." An early record is "John of Akyne ('of’ here evidently an error), a Scottish
merchant, petitioned for the return of his ship and goods illegally seized in England in 1405 ..."

Alexd. and Alexr. See Alexander.
Derived "From [the] Greek ..., defender of man. Miss Yonge has pointed out in her History of
Christian names that nowhere is the name Alexander so thoroughly national as in Scotland, into
which country it was introduced by Queen Margaret, wife of King Malcolm Ceanmor, from the
Hungarian Court, where she was brought up. 'Her third son was the first of the three Alexanders,
under whom the country spent her most prosperous days. The death of the last was a signal for
the long death-feud between the northern and southern kingdoms, and all the consequent
miseries' ... So popular indeed became the name in Scotland that Alexander in its diminutive
form 'Sandy' is even more the national name than 'Donald.' " An early record is "William
Alexander was connected with the accounts of the city of Edinburgh in 1435 ..."

more probably it is 'son of Ellis,' q.v. Lower (s.v. Alison) says: 'It may be remarked that the
vulgar pronunciation of Ellis in the south is exactly the same as that of the fema le personal name
Alice.' (2) In some few cases "Alison and Allison may be forms of Allanson. In 1559 a woman
Jonet Alysone was also referred to as Jonet Alaneson ..."Black discounts another possibility as
"... too sweeping." An early record is "Patrick Alissone del counte de Berewyk rendered
homage, 1296 ..."

Variants of the surname Alan. "This name in Scotland is of twofold origin: (1) from the Old
Gaelic name Ailéne (the Ailenus of Adamnan ...) or Ailin, from ail 'rock' seen in the old name of
Dumbarton (Ail Cluade, 'rock of the Clyde). From this source comes Alwyn, the name of the
first earls of Levenax, early confused with OE. [Old English] Aelwin. (2) from the Breton
through NF. [Norman French] Alan. An early record is "Alan, son of Waldeve witnessed
charters by King David I, 1139 ..."

A variant of the surname Allanson. The name means " 'The son of Allan,' q.v. Rendered in
Latin documents by genitive Alani." An early record is "Reginald filius [son of] Alani was a
burgess of Aberdeen in 1317 ..."
Allanesone , Johne, G., be r. of w. Mariota, dr. of umq. Thos. Gray 11 Mar. 1528-9

The name is "Of territorial origin from the old barony of Allardice in the parish of Arbuthnott,
Kincardineshire. 'It is not a very common name, but all who hold it believe in their descent form
the old family which was settled for so long a period on the banks of the Bervie Water' " An
early record is "Alexander de Allyrdas, who witnessed a charter of the lands of Glack c. [about]
1294 ..."

"This surname, from the baptismal name Andrew (in Greek Aindreas, 'manly') is common in
Scotland both as forename and as a surname. ... In the Highlands the name was early adopted in
appearing Gaelic as Aindrea, ..." An early record is "Andreas, clericus Moraviensis, in record, a.
1242 ..."

The name is "Of territorial origin from the old lands of Anstruther in Fife. William de Candela
was possessed of the barony at his death in 1153. His son, also named William, was a beneficiary
of Balmerino Abbey sometime after 1165. These de Candelas were of the Norman family of
Malherbe, who held the lands of Candel in Dorset in capite in the eleventh and twelfth centuries.
Henry, son of the second William de Candela, appears to have been the first to assume the
territorial designation of Anstruther. As Henricus de Ainestrother he witnessed the gift of
fifteen acres of Balmulinauch (Balmerino) to the church of St. Andrews by Adam de Stawell
before 1225 ..."

The name has two origins: "(1) a diminutive of Augustine ('majestic'), the name of the great
Father of the Church, Augustinus of Hippo, ... (2) an Englishing of Uisdean (Hùisdean) 'one of
the many instances in which classical names are utilised to represent Gaelic names of somewhat
similar sound' ... The Austins appear first on record as allies and supporters of the Keiths. The
name was variously spelt, though in ancient records it was generally begun with Ou or Ow." An
early record is "... in 1587 of the name of Alexander Ousteane, burgess of Edinburgh, as one of
the cautioners for George Keith, Earl Marshall, in an action raised against him by Margaret
Erskine, Lady Pitcarie."

A variant of the surname Baad. “There is a place named Baad near Stirling, and lands of the
same name are recorded in Perthsire in 1544 ... From the references the former locality seems to
have been the parent of the surname. In Aberdeenshire there is a place named Baad (in parish of
Peterculter), a Bad (obsolete place name in Cairnie), and Baud (in Birse), all from Gaelic bad, a
cluster, thicket, and by extension of meaning, a hamlet.” An early record is “John Bad a charter
witness 1498 ...”

Caution! The two names Baird and Bard are probably hopelessly mixed. Black states “The name
[Bard] has most probably become lost in Baird.” “This name [Baird] appears to be territorial in
origin. A family ‘de Bard’ or ‘de Barde’ held considerable land in Lanarkshire from the family
of de Bigres.” An early record is “Henry de Ba rde witnessed the gift by Thomas de Haya to the
House of soltre between 1202-28 ...”

The name is “Of local or territorial origin from the lands of Balmain in the parish of Fettercairn,
Kincardineshire. The place name is from the Gaelic Baile meadhon, ‘middle town,’ and the
surname if Englished would be ‘Middleton.’ From the scant references in record to this name it
is probable that the family became extinct in the main line or that they parted with their
patrimonial estate at an early period.” An early record is “In 1553 Patrik Balmen took the part of
‘ye mekle devill’ in a mediaveval play in Perth ...”

Bannatyne. See Ballantyne .

Black mentions some “... popularly believed ...” origins for the name, but states “... I know of no
evidence in support [of the beliefs]” “The first authentic reference to the family is in a charter by
David II (1368) granting to Dovinaldus Banerman, the king’s physician, the lands of the two
Clynteys of Clyntreys (Clinterty), and the two Achrinys (now an obsolete place name), namely
Watirton and Welton near Aberdeen ...”

Variants of the surname Baron. “Baron usually meant one who held his lands from the king by
military service, but there are many instances of persons being called barons who held of subject
superiors, the ‘Bissets Barrones’ of Lovat for example. In other instances ‘Barons’ were just
landowners who had a certain amount of jurisdiction over the populations on their lands. ... The
name here [Angus?] probably originated from the small baronies attached to the Abbey of
Coupar-Angus. Thus the tenant of the barony of Glenisla became Robert Barrone, tennant of
Glennylay, 1508 ...”

“This surname, as shown by the examples quoted is merely a variant of the name Bartholomew
...” Some early records are Alisaundre Bertholmeu of the county of Edinburgh rendered homage
in 1296 ... In 1343 William Bertylmen rendered to Exchequer the account of the provost ... of
Edinburgh ...In the preceding year the same individual, as William Bartholomei, was rewarded
for his share in the capture of Edinburgh Castle ... A second payment was made to him in 1343
when his name occurs in the form Bertilmen ... A fourth spelling of his name occurs in 1368
when he referred to as ‘Willelmus Bertilmew in burgo de Edynburgche’ “

“This surname comes form the occupation of ‘bakester,’ originally a woman that baked, OE.
[Old English] bæcestre a female baker. In Middle English the ending - estre being unstressed
soon lost its final e, and -ster came to be regarded as an emphatic form of -er, and consequently
was applied to men as well as women, so that the early Middle English feminine bakstere
became later Middle English masculine baxster. In Latin charters the word or name is rendered
pistor.” Two early records are “Between 1153 and 1177 William pistor witnessed a grant by
David Olifard to the Hospital of Soltre ... Between 1200-1240 Reginald Baxtar witnessed the gift
of the church of Wemys in Fife to Soltre ...”

Variants of the surname Beaton. “Two learned families named Macbeth and Beaton or Bethune
practised medicine in the Isles in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Their names in the
seventeenth and eighteenth centuries became merged in English in the one surname of Beaton.
The Macbeths practised in Islay and Mull, and the Beatons in Skye.” ... “The first of the Islay
family on record is Fercos Macbetha, who witnessed and probably wrote the Gaelic charter of
1408.” ... “The Mull Beatons or Betons were hereditary physicians to the Macleans of
Dowart. In 1572 Hector MacLaine of Dowart granted a charter to Andrew MacDonil Vikinollif
(i.e. son of the doctor) and his heirs of the pennyland of Piencross [Pennycross] and Brolas for
his skill in the medical art.” ... “The Beatons of Skye ‘were real Beatons or Bethunes from Fife,
descended from the Lairds of Balfour. A grandson of the fifth laird, Dr. Peter Bethune, settled in
Skye about the middle of the sixteenth century. ...’ “

Belhaven, Lord, B. and G., gratis, by act of C. 18 Aug. 1736

“Three derivitives are possible for this name: (1) as a descriptive sobriquet, Peter le Bel (‘the
handsome,’from OF. [Old French] bel, handome, beautiful), found in the English Hundred Rolls;
(2) of local origin, as ME. [Middle English] ‘John atte Belle’ or ‘Richard atte Bell’ (not
uncommon in ME. registers) from the sign of his public house; (3) as a metronymic, ‘Robert fil
Bell,’ meaning Robert, the son of Bell or Isabel. 1 and 2 are I think, the chief parents of the
name.” An early record is “John Bell appears as a notary in St. Andrews, 1248 ...”

A variant of the surname Belsches. Derived from the barony of the same name in the lordship of
Jedburgh, Roxburghshire, which belonged to the monks of Jedburgh. The barony may have been
named by some earlier owner from Belasis (so spelled also in 1305) in Northumberland, Bellasis
(1345) in Durham or from Bellasis which is near Coulommières in Seine-et-Marne department,
France.” An early record is “The seal of Richard de Belchis is appended to his homage of 1296
...”

Sancto Edmundo, witnessed a charter of sale of land in Perth, 1219 ... John Benet, Scotsman, late
an enemy, became liegeman of Henry IV of England, 1402 ...”

Variants of the surname Beveridge. “A well-known surname in Fife, where it is pronounced
Berridge or Berritch. Mr. Beveridge ... says the origin of the name is to be found in ‘Beverege,’
the name of an island in the Severn referred to by Florence of Worcester as a retreat of the Danes
during a revolt of the English. The name he correctly says means ‘Beaver Island,’ from OE. [Old
English] befer or beofer, and ig or ige, island.” “The earliest mention of the name in Scottish
record is in 1302 when Walter Beverage is named as juror on an inquest at St. Andrews
...”

“The surname is a personal one, a diminutive of bis, OF. [Old French] for ‘rock dove.’ ... Sir
Thomas Gray ... states that William the Lion in 1174, on his return from captivity in Falaise and
in England, brought back young Englishmen of family to seek their fortune in the Scottish Court;
and among these were named the ‘Biseys’ ... The first of the name recorded in Scotland is
Henricus Byset, who witnessed a charter by William the Lion granted before 1198 ...”

“ ‘A great difficulty with the Black-names’ says Harrison, ‘is the impossibility in many cases of
deciding whether the etymon is the OE. [Old English] blæc, blac, ‘black,’ or the OE. blác,
‘bright,’ ‘white,’ ‘pale.’ Normally blæc, blac, yields ‘black,’ and blác should give ‘blake’ (or
‘bloke’); but the forms are inextricably confused and the present spelling is often no guide to the
pronunciation past or present.’ ... In early Scots Latin charters the name is rendered Niger.” Two
early records are “Hugh Niger appears as a charter witness in Fife between 1200-1210 ... Adam
the Black was one of the jurors on an inquisition held at Lanark in 1303 ...”

Variants of the surname Boston. “The Bostons of Gattonside are an old Border family, and their
name appears in record as Boustoune and Bowstone. There is a town named Boston in
Lincolnshire, but the Scottish name may be of local origin.” An early record is “Bernard
Boustoun was one of the witnesses to a charter by Andrew, abbot of Melrose, 1540 ...”

Derived “From the lands of Bowden in Roxburghshire. ‘For a period of about two hundred years
various persons of the same surname are witnesses to a number of charters [in the chartulary of
Kelso]. These are not mentioned as holding lands in the parish, but would appear to have been
kindly tenants of the monastery who took their name from the barony. The monks of different
periods were in the practice of sub- letting the lands of the barony, and some of the lands, on
whatever condition originally let, came at length to be held by the parties in hereditary right’
...” An early record is “Between c. 1200 and c. 1240 one or more individuals named Richard de
Boulden witnessed charters ...”

Derived “(1) From the old manor of Bower in the parish of Drummelzier, Peeblesshire. ... (2) A
shortening of bowmaker, q.v. Before the invention of gunpowder a bowmaker was an honorable
and lucrative profession. In Edinburgh the bowmakers in the seventeenth century were known as
‘Bowers.’ “ Two early records are “Lorence atte Bure of the county of Peebles, and William
Oftherebure of the county of Roxburgh rendered homage, 1296. ... Walter Bower or
Bowmaker, abbot of Inchcolme, was continuator of John of Fordun’s Scottish Chronicle.”

“Innes ... says this name means a man in charge of the bow or cattle, and in his Legal antiquities
... he defines bowman as ‘a person who farms for a season the tenant’s milk cows, and the
pasture to maintain them,’ and James Macdonald ... after referring to Inne’s definition says ‘The
sheriff is no doubt strictly correct as to the primary meaning and use of the term, but so far as I
have observed, ‘bowman’ is used in various parts of the country to designate small farmers and
occasionally farm servants.’ I rather think that the name has the same meaning as Bower and
Bowmaker.” An early record is “In 1328 Gregory Bovman who rendered to Exchequer the
accounts of the sheriff of Aberdee ... appears as Gregory dictus Bowman in an inquisition in
Aberdeen in 1333 ...”

“This surname may be derived from the name of the island of Bute, in G. [Gaelic] Bod. The

Variants of the surname Boyce. Derived “From AF. del Bois, ‘in or by the wood,’ Latinized in
early charters de Bosco. ... The s was preserved as a voiceless consonant, and the name rhymes
with voice and choice.” An early record is “Hugo Delboys witnessed a confirmation charter by
Hugh, bishop of St. Andrews, between 1185-88 ...”

“The name of a family which once possessed extensive territories on the south side of Edinburgh
and took their surname from their lands. The first of the name recorded is Henry de Brade, who
appears in the middle of the twelfth century as owner of not only the Braid Hills, but also of
Blackford Hill, the Plewlands, and Bavelaw. He was sherrif of Edinburgh in the reign of William
the Lion ... and [appeared] as Henricus de Brade, marescallus, ...”

Variants of the surname Bremner. “The old form was Brabener, ‘the Brabander,’ i.e., a native of
Brabant. ... Artificers and traders from the Low Countries of the continent settled in
Aberdeenshire and elsewhere on the East Coast at an early date. ‘The braboner, or webster craft,
or weaver trade, holds the eighth pace amongst the nine trades’ of Dundee ...” An early record is
“Walter Brabounare held tenement in Irvine, Ayrshire, in 1418-1426 ...”

Brooksbanks, Stamp, Esq., B. and G., gratis, for good services, by act of C. 12 Nov. 1755

The origin of the name is “Local. There are places so named near Hawick, and in the shires of
Ayr, Dumfries, Clackmannan, and Banff.” An early record is “John Brume was one of the
burgesses of Stirling who attacked the cruives and fishings of the abbot and convent of
Cambuskenneth, 1366 ...”
Broome , Capt. Benjamin, B. and G. (in M.T.C. 3 Feb. 1654, Groome) 3 Feb. 1654
Derived “From the lands of Brothirstanys (now Brotherstone) in East Lothian, granted by
Malcolm IV to the hospital of Soutra ... Those of the name residing around Gordon, Earlston,
and Smailholm, may derive their surname from Brotherstones near St. boswells.” An early
record is “Between 1153 and 1177 Hugh de Brothirstane witnessed a grant by David Olifard to
the hospital of Soltra ...”

Brotonne , Thos., B. and G., s. and h. of umq. Thos. B. 24 Mar. 1516-17

The name is “An old surname in Orkney, dreived from either Overbrough or Netherbrough in
Harray.” An early record is “Thomas Burgh, witness in Harray in 1530 may be the Thomas
Burcht, withness at the Kirk of Harray in 1557 ...”

Broughton, Thomas, Esq., B. and G., gratis, by act of C. 21 Jan. 1726
„ Thomas, one of H.M. Commissioners of Excise in Scotland, B. and G., gratis, by act of C.
  5 Jan. 1728
“A very common name in Scotland, of more than one origin. (1) Brun is a common personal
name in OE. charters, e.g. Brun, c. 970, Brun bydel (‘beadle’), c. 1000 ... The name is from an
old adjective meaning ‘brown, dark red,’ OE. And OHG. brun, ON. brunn. The adjective was
also borrowed from OHG. into old French and is the source of the French surname Le Brun. ...
(2) From G. Mac a’bhriutainn, from britheamhain, the former G. genitive of britheamh, ‘brehon,
breive, judge.’ “ An early record of the first is “Gamel, son of Brun came into possession of
Bothel (now Bootle) in the time of Henry I (1100-1135).” An early record from the second is
“M’ aBruin is on of the witnesses in the unique Gaelic charter of 1408 ...”

record was “A payment was made to Ade de Brunhill in 1359 ...”

A variant of Brownlea. The name is “Of local origin, perhaps from Brownlee in Lanarkshire.
There is also a Brownlee near Dundonald, Ayrshire.” An early record is “ ‘Wedow’ Brownlee
was tenant on lands under Newbotle Abbey in 1563 ...”

A variant of Brownrigg. The name is “Of local origin from some small place of the name. The
lands of Alanshaw had as one boundary Burnerig (now Brounrig) in the time of Alan the
Steward ...”

,, Thomas, B., cuik, the dewtie thairof gevin to him gratis at the requeist of ane noble lord James,
   erl of Arrane, chancellar, provest of this burgh 27 Nov. 1584
“This name, so celebrated in the history of Scotland, is of territorial origin, from the Château
d’Adamat Brix, between Cherbourg and Valognes, Normandy. The ruins of the extensive
fortress built in the eleventh century by Adam de Brus and called after him Château d’Adam yet
remain. The first Robert de Brus on record in Britain was probably the leader of the Brus
contingent in the army of William the Conqueror in 1066. He appears to have died about the year
1094. A son of this Robert de Brus, known as Robert le Meschin or the cadet, was the
first of his family connected with Scotland.”

The origin of the name is “Local. From Bruntsfield, a former suberb of Edinburgh, now
incorporated within the city. Previous to the place taking its present name it was known as
Brounisfield ... from an early owner, Richard Broune of Boroumore, who held the lands in the
fourteenth century.” An early record is “Adam Bruntfield fought a duel with James Carmichael
in 1597 over the murder of his brother, Stephen Bruntfield, merchant in Edinburgh ...”

The origin of the name is “Local. There is a Brunstane on Brunstane Burn, Midlothian, and there
is a village of Brunton in the parish of Criech, Fife.” An early record is “... Walter of Burntoun
held part of Luffness in the reign of Robert III ...”

Brussat, Noye (Anthony), G., sururgus (surgeon), F.C. 4 Sept. 1549

A variant of Brian. “A well known personal name of common occurrence in Breton records
from the ninth century. It is a derivative from some full name compounded with bri ‘dignity,’
‘esteem’ ... The name was introduced into Britain by Bretons who were among the Normans in
the invasion of England.” An early record is “Linaldus filius Brian is mentioned in reign of
William the Lion ...”
Bryan, Johne, B. and G., gentleman, gratis, “ English “ 10 May 1654
Derived “From Bricius, a Gaulish saint of the fifth century, nephew of S. Martin of Tours, whom
he succeeded in the bishopric there. A common personal name in Scots records at end of twelfth
and beginning of thirteenth centuries.” An early record is “Bricius, judex, c. 1189-99, witnessed
a charter by Laurence, son of Orm de Abernethy ...”

A variant of Bryde . “Brydie is an old surname in the parish of Lochwinnoch, and in modern
times the spelling has been changed to Brodie ..., and Breadie and Broddie are given as variants
of the name in DPD [the diocese and presbytery of Dunkeld] ...” An early record is “Dovenald
Bryd, burgess of Perth, rendered homage, 1296 ...”

“This surname has nothing to do with the name Bullock, though doubtless the names have been
confused in early times. Bulloch is simply Balloch, and practically all of the name come from or
originated in the parish of baldernock, Stirlingshire ... In old records the form Balloch was
almost invariably used until the miccle of the eighteenth centur y. The Ballochs or Bullochs were
ranked or included as a sept of the Macdonalds.”

A variant of Burness. “This surname is said to occur in England in early times, but the Scottish
Burness is most probably of local origin. Burneshead, Cumberland was the seat of a family of
Burnes up to the reign of Edward I ... Robert Burns’s right name was Burness (pron. Bur’ness
not Burness’) but because the name was pronounced in Ayrshire as if written Burns, he and his
brother Gilbert agreed to drop Burness and assume Burns in April 1786 ...”

Derived “From G. ceard, a craftsman, an artist mechanic, and later a travelling tinker. In an
ancient Irish manuscript cerdd is glossed by Latin aerarius ... which means ‘worker in brass.’
Many of the fine old Highland plaid brooches of brass, specimens of which are shown in the
Scottish National Museum of Antiquities in Edinburgh, are believed to be the work of men of
this class. Spalding in his Memorialls ... referring to an officer in the regiment of the Master of
Forbes says: ‘This captain’s true name was Forbes, but nick- named Kaird, because when he
was a boy he served a kaird’ ...” An early record is “In 1275 Gilfolan Kerd, a mariner in the
service of Alexander de Argadia, was with others arrested at Bristol on suspicion of piracy ...”

“This surname is of twofold origin, - Lowland and Highland. The name of the Camerons of the
Lowlands is of territorial origin, from one of three places so named: (1) Cameron near
Edinburgh; (2) Cameron in Lennox; (3) Cameron (of old, Camberone), a parish in Fife, the
principal if not the only source of the Lowland surname. ... The Highland clan name, like that of
Campbell, is derived from a facial deformity, cam-shròn, Gaelic for ‘wry’ or ‘hook nose.’ The
late Rev. Dr. Joass of Golspie stated that a hooked nose was a characteristic of the old Clan
Cameron families ...” “Of the Lowland Camerons the first in record is Adam de Kamerum who
witnessed a charter of ‘vnum rete super matricem aquam de Thei’ (Tay) by David de Haya to the
monks of Cupar between 1214-49 ...” “The Clan Cameron consisted of three main branches, (1)
Macmartins of Letterfinlay ... (2) Macgillonies of Strone; and (3) Macsorlies of Glen-Nevis.”

Cammack, James, carriers’ porter, Candlemaker Row, B. 3 May 1841
Derived from the “G. Caimbeul, ‘wry (or crooked) mouth,’ a name probably applied to some
early chief of the clan. ... The name may simply mean ‘with arched lips.’ ... In a charter of 1447
... the name Campbell seems then to have been recognized as no more than a nickname. In this
charter by the first Lord Campbell he is styled ‘Duncan le Cambell,’ where le is the lie so
commonly used in Scottish charters to denote that what follows is in the vernacular, and may be
translated ‘as we say,’ or ‘so called,’ ... Clan tradition represents the Campbells as being
originally known as Cla nn Duibhne or O’Duine from a certain Diarmid O’Duine of Lochow. As
the O’Duines, and therfore the Campbells also, were traditionally said to be of the Siol Diarmid,
the Fingalian hero who slew the wild boar, it is to be noted that the father of Diarmid was named
Fergus Cerr-beoil, ‘wry-mouth.’ “

Canham, John, Esq., mt. in London, B. and G., by act of C. 6 Dec. 1752

Variants of the surname Cannan. The derivation of the name is “Probably from Ir. O’Canáin,
descendant of Canán (diminutive of Cano, a wolf-cub). “ An early record is “Fergus Acannane
had sasine of lands in the parish of Balmakclellane, 1562 ...”
Cannan, Thomson, woollen draper, B., as p. to Andrew Scott, mt. (p. same day as from
  11 Nov. 1811) 3 June 1825
Cannon, Alexr., printer, B. and G., as p. to Wm. Reid, printer and bookseller, Leith (p. same day
  as from 1 Mar. 1822) 11 Feb. 1841

“A writer in the Scottish antiquary (IV) says that the name occurs in the Exchequer Rolls in the
fifteenth century, and that the family, by trade dealers in cloth, supplied the king’s household.
They were eveidently, he says, Fleming, and are mentioned in connection with Flanders. they
obtained land at Masterton near Dunfermline, which their descendants of the name still possess.”
An early record is “Adam Cant was bailie there [Edinburgh], 1403 ...”

Chamblet, Wm., B., wauker 7 May 1533

Derived “From the office [of chamberlain], OF. chamberlenc, Latin camerarius. The office of
royal chamberlain, was one of great responsibility in virtue of the fact that until the reign of
James I he managed the king’s revenue and was head of the Exchequer. The great nobles, also,
had each a chamberlain who looked after his lord’s business affairs.” An early record is “John
Camerarius witnessed a confirmation charter by William the Lion, c. 1175 ...”

,, Joseph, B. and G., servant to the Lord Balantyne, by r. of w. Marie, dr. to umq.

,, Peter, B. and G., Esquer, gratis 14 July 1693
Chamberlain, Peter, captain of the “Advice” (R.N.), B. and G. 19 Mar. 1708

Derived “From the office of ‘chancellor,’ either civil or ecclesiastical; an official who kept
registers of an order of knighthood, an ecclesiastical judge. An ancient family of this name in
Lanarkshire were vassals of the lords of Somerville before 1432. They have possessed Shieldhill

Variants of the surname Chapman. “This surname, found mainly in the Lothians and Perthsire,
is derived from the occupation of ‘chapman,’ OE. ceapman, ‘merchant.’ It is probable, as
Bardsley says, that the early chapman was stationary and dealt in a much larger way than we
now suppose. The chapman portrayed in Burns’s Tam o’ Shanter was of a lower grade. The
earliest occurence of the name seems to be in 1296 when a pardon was granted to a man for
causing the death of Ralph Chepman, provost of Aberdeen in 1327 ...”

hereditary in a family called from the office de Capella, and was attached to a third part of the
lands of Craigmillar ...” An early record is “In 1328 there is entry of wages of the boys of
William de Capella ...”

Variants of the surname Child. Derived “From the OE. personal name Cild. The ‘exact sense of
the name is uncertain. The singular is used as a title of honour in late OE. times and this found
also throught the Middle Ages, as in Childe Roland’ ... It was synonymous with enfant in
France.” An early record is “Henricus Child was canon of Scone c. 1275 ...”

Variants of the surname CLELAND. “This surname is supposed to be derived from lands named
Cleland or Kneland in the parish of Dalziel, Lanarkshire. ... Anderson ... says there are several
instances of Cleland of Cleland being called Knieland of that Ilk; ... The name may be an early
corruption of Cleveland.” “The first of the family in record is said to be Alexander Kneland of
that Ilk, temp. Alexander III.”

“The Clephanes appear to have been an offshoot of an ancient family in England which derived
their surname from Clapham in Sussex, where they appear to have been settled shortly after the
Conquest. The first of the family in Scotland settled in Lauderdale as a vassal of the Morvilles.”
An early record is “Alan de Clapham witnessed a charter by Roland of Galloway, c. 1200 ...”

Variants of the surname Clerihew. “An Aberdeenshire surname.” An early record is “William
Clerihew of Kegge was convicted of profanation of the Lord’s day, etc., in 1644 ...”

Variants of the surname Clark. The word “Originally [meant] a man in a religious order, and
later a scholar, a penman, in early charters Latinized clericus. An early record is Roger clericus
held a land between 1174-78 ...”

Variants of the surname Clarkson. Clarkson means “ ‘the son of the clerk’ (i.e. scholar). See
Clark.” An early record is “Thomas Clerkson de Aldane was a forestaller in Aberdeen in 1402
...”

Variants of the surnames Colden and Cowden. The two surnames appear to have been mixed by
the editors. Colden/Coldane is derived “From the lands of Cowden near Dalkeith, Midlothian.”
An early record is “David Colden who appears as notary in St. Andrews diocese, 1459 ... may be
David Coldane, succentor of Dunkeld, 1492 ...” Cowden is derived “From Cowden in the parish
of Dalkeith, Midlothian. There is also a Cowden near Dollar, but Cowden near Dalkeith is
more probable source of the name.” An early record is “Joneta Cowden, heir of William
Cowden, burgess of Edinburgh, 1595 ...”

The name is “Local. There is Colston near Bishopriggs, Lanarkshire, and Colstoun in East
Lothian. Colstane in Aberdeenshire in local speech is a contraction of Codilstan (in Logie-
Codilstane) now Logie-Coldstone.” An early record is “Robert Colston, a Scotsman, had a safe
conduct in England, 1465 ...”

A variant of the surname Coltart. The name is “Explained as from Coltard = Colt herd, OE. colt
+ hierde. Of the Coultharts of Galloway a ridiculous genealogy has been published, in which the
family are traced to one Coulthartus, a Roman soldier who fought in the battle of Mons
Graupius! The local pronunciation in the Stewartry is Cowtart. Lower says probably from
Coudhart, a village in the department of Orne, NE. of Argentan in Normandy. He says the name
is no doubt territorial as it is written with ‘de’ in the thriteenth and fourteenth centuries.” An
early record is “Alan Colthird witnessed the sealing of an inquest at Berwick anent
a fishing on the Tweed in 1467 ...”

A variant of the surname Conn. “An old name in Aberdeenshire, where there was a prominent
Roman Catholic family of the name, Con or Cone of Auchry, in the parish of Monquhitter. They
claimed to be a branch of the Clan Donald ... the surname being assumed from the traditional
name of the Clan, ‘Siol Cuin’ or ‘Con.’ The family were driven into exile soon after 1642 ... In
the birth brieve of Gilbert Chalmer, 1650, the Cons or cones of auchry are said to be descended
from William Con [five generations earlier] ‘lauchfull sone to Donnald of the Iles and Kyntyr,
chief of the Mackdonald’ ...”
Con, John, G. (Con’s Cl. is probably named from him) 1 Apr. 1517

“In the time of the Roman Empire the position of Comes stabuli, ‘count of the stable,’ was an
office of dignity. Transferred to the court of the Frankish kings, the title became one word,
Comestabulus, and after the eighth century was changed to conestabulus, as the name of the
officer entrusted with the charge of cavalry. By the thirteenth century the title of Constable (OF.
conestable) was given to the commander of all the forces. In Scotland to the Constable was
‘entrusted the guard of the king’s person and of his dwelling and the maintenance of the king’s
peace for twelve leagues around the place where he might be in residence, with the arrest and
trial of offenders within this limit.’ ... The surname in Scotland is not common, and is without
doubt from the more humble office of town constable or peace officer.” An early record is
“Thomas Cunstabil, witness in Lanark, 1490 ...”

between 1219-37 ...” Cowie on the other hand is “Local from one or other of places of the name
but mainly from the ancient barony of Cowie in Kincardineshire.” An early record is “Herbert de
Cowy witnessed a charter by Nicholas de Dumfries in 1394 ...”

“COWAN, Cowans, Cowen. Common surnames in Ayrshire, Dumfriesshire, and other Lowland
counties. (1) Sometimes explained as from Scots cowan, a drystonediker, but I doubt this
explandation. (2) It may be a corruption of colquhoun, the common pronunciation of which is
Cohoon. Mr. Alexander Cowan, father of Sir John Cowan of Beeslack is said to have left on
record that many of his grandfather’s books bore the name of Colquhoun. (3) In the south
Highlands the ‘Mac’ of Macillechomhghain disappears from the name and in Argyllshire, e.g.
Iain MacCòmhain becomes Iain Còmhan in Gaelic while the English equivalent is Cowan.” An
early record is “The name of James Cowhen, chaplain in North Berwick, 1560...”

A variant of Creamer. Derived “From the occupation. Sir John Skene (1681) says: ‘Ane pedder

Dundee market.’ “

Variants of the surname Creech. Derived “From Creich in Fifeshire, where a family of this name
rented land for several generations. ‘The parish of Creich, in the northern part of Fifeshire,
contains the remains of an ancient castle but there is no trace of any family bearing the name
occupying the lands’ ...” An early record is “Douenaldus (i.e. Donald) de Creych, a cleric, was
one of the witnesses to a confirmation charter by Walter, son of Alan of the land of Tubermor
between 1204 and 1241 ...”

“A surname derived from an occupation, G. criathrar, generally rendered (the miller’s) ‘sifter,’
but more correctly translated ‘sievewright.’ It is the name of a small sept at one time fairly
numerous in Strathspey and Lochtayside. They are ranked as Mackintoshes and some persons of
the name in the United States now call themselves Mackintosh ...” An early record is Hohn
McAchrerar had half of Balinlagan, 1541 ...”

Variants of the surname Crichton. The name is “Of territorial origin from the old barony of
Chrichton in Midlothian. The old spellings of the barony name are various, but one, Kreiton,
‘seems to settle how the name was pronounced’ ...” An early record is “Turstan de Crectune
witnessed King David’s great charter to Holyrood. c. 1128 ...”

The name is derived “From residence at or near a roadside cross or crucifix, ME. crouche. The

left the name of ‘cross’ and ‘crouch’ upon many localities, especially in the South of England ‘
...” An early record is “Johannes Crooch witnessed a confirmation charter by Alexander Cumyn,

Cruickbane (Crukbain), Bernard, glover, B., as p. to Bernard Ross, skinner, B. 27 June 1739

“With the possible exception of the first record of this name, which may point to a nickname, I
do not think this surname has any connection with bowleggedness or ‘crooked shanks.’ The
earliest spellings of the name, with the one exception noted, are always in the singular. The two
counties with which the name is most intimately connected are Kincardine and Aberdeen, and in
the former we have the river Cruick rising in the parish of Fearn and joining the North Esk near
the Kirk of Stracathro. The word ‘Cruick’ is found several times in combination in Scots
place names, i.e. ‘Cruikitheuch’ ... ‘the crukit aiker’ ... Cruiktheugh, later ... Cruikhaugh at
Inverbervie. “Shank’ is also a common element in Scots place names, either alone or in
combination, i.e. Schank (in Midlothian, whence the surname Shank or Schank); Shankend,
Shankfoot, etc. In toponymy ‘shank’ has the meaning of ‘projecting point of a hill joining it to
the plain.’ The surname may thus quite well be of local origin - the shank on the Cruick or the
Cruick-shank.” An early record is “John Crokeshanks, burgess of Haddington, rendered
homage, 1296 ...”

“The once powerful family of Comyn or Cumyn are believed to have come from the town of
Comines near Lille on the frontier between France and Belgium, though there is no positive
evidence in favor of this view. The name is always written without ‘de’ in early Scots records.”
“The first of the name connected with Scotland is Willelmus Comyn, a churchman, chancellor to
David I. He was promoted to the bishopric of Durham by the Empress Matilda, but had many
controversies with his clergy. Later he was poisoned by some of their number who mixed poison
with the wine of the Sacrament and gave it to him to drink.”

Variants of the surname Cuningham. The name is “Of territorial origin from the northern
district of the name in Ayrshire. ... Wernebald, a vassal of Hugh de Moreville, obtained the
manor and vill of Cunningham from his feudal superior. ... Robert filius Wernebaldi granted the
church of Kilmaurs with half a carucate of land belonging thereto to the monks of Kelso, c. 1170,
and the grant was confirmed by his superior, Robert de Moreville, and by Robert, son of Robert,
son of Wernebaldus ...” An early record is “Richard de Cunningham appears as witness to
charter by Alan, son of Roland, Constable of Scotland, between 1210-33 ...”

Variants of Currie. The surname is “(1) a variant of CORRIE, q.v. Although there is a place
named Currie in Midlothian there is no evidence of its having given origin to a surname.” An
early record is “Philip de Curry granted the lands of Dalhengun and Bargower in Kyle to the
Abbey of Melrose, 1179 ...” The name is also “(2) A modification of MACVURICH, q.v.” An
example of this variant is “The minister at Row, Dumbartonshire, 1709-19, was known as Rev.
Archibald Currie or M’Currie.”
Curie, Jas., B. and G., as s. and h. of umq. Jas. C., F.C. 16 Jan. 1548-9

Variants of the surname Cuthbert . The name is “An OE. personal name meaning ‘bright
champion.’ The popularity of this surname in the Lothians and in the north of England is due to
the great saint of Lindisfarne after whom the town of Kirkcudbright was named. A church
dedicated to S. Cuthbert in Dryfesdale was granted to Jocelin, bishop of Glasgow in 1174. The
common pronunciation of the saint’s name over the whole north of England is invariably
Cudbert, from which comes the diminutives ‘Cuddie’ and ‘Cuddy.’ “ An early record is “Paton
Cudbert and Thom Cudbert were tenants in the Grange of Kerso in 1466 ...”

Variants of the surname Dalgleish. The name is “Of territorial origin from the lands of Dalgleish
above the sources of Tinna Water in the parish of Ettrick, Selkirkshire. Individuals of this name
on the border figure constantly in the public records as disturbers of the peace.” An early record
is “Symon de Dalgles in 1407 witnessed a charter by Robert, duke of Albany in favor of John de
Hawdene of the lands of Hawdene and Yethame ...”

Variants of the surname Dalyell. The name is “Of territorial origin from the old barony of
Dalziel in Lanarkshire. The names [DALYELL, Dalyiel, Dalzell, Dalziel] are pronounced
‘Diyell’ or simply DL. some of the name, however call themselves Dal- yell, some Dal-zell, and
some Dal- zeel. ... The first of the name appears in 1259 when the baron of Daliel served on an
inquest ...”

Variants of the surname Dennistoun. The name is “Of territorial origin from the old barony of
Danzielstoun in the parish of Kilmalcolm, Renfrewshire. The manor took its name from some
man named Daniel, and it bore this name as early as the reign of Malcom IV ... The statement of
Buchanan of auchmar that the family sprang from a younger branch of the old earls of Lennox is
more than doubtful.” An early record is “Sir Huew of Danielestoun of Lanarkshire rendered
homage in 1296.

Variants of the surname Darroch. “People named Darroch were at one time common in Islay
and Jura, and were counted a sept of Clan Donald. (1) The Stirling Darrochs derive from the
place named Darroch near Falkirk. (2) The name may also be from adjectival form of a lost
MacDara, ‘son of oak.’ ... Macc Dara in the Book of Armagh. With ‘son of oak,’ cf.
MacCarthainn, ‘son of Rowan’ (tree). See also MacDhubhdara. (3) Popular tradition in the West
Highlands is that the name is from Dath riabhach, a shortening of Mac ‘Ille riabhach, but this
seems doubtful.”

“The origin of this surname is found in the office of ‘judex’ or ‘dempster’ to the Parliament,
shire, or baron-bailie. Until the year 1747 every laird whose land had been erected into a barony
was empowered to hold courts for the trial and punishment of certain offenders within his
barony; and the dempster was part of his retinue.” An early record is “The name of Haldan de
Emester of Perthshire, who rendered homage in 1296 ... is to be read Haldan Deemester.”

Variants of the surname Denholm. Derived “From the old barony of Denholm, in the parish of
Cavers, Roxburghshire. The name may also be from Denholm, a parish in Dumfriesshire, in
which county there were landowners of the name in the fifteenth century ... but the first is the
more likely source of the name.” An early record is “Guy de Denum of Roxburghshire rendered
homage, 1296, ...”

“The old family of this name in Ross-shire were descended from Duncan Campbell, one of the
Campbells of Lochow, who to escape from justice for certain offences committed by him fled
with his brother to the north, where he settled. Both assumed their mother’s name of Dunune ...”
an early record is “Mariot Denune was made heir of her brother, John Denune, 1416 ...”

an official designation which afterwards became a family name. In mediæval times the deoradh
was the person who had custody of the relic of a saint. ... (2) Of territorial origin from Dewar in
the parish of Heriot, Midlothian.” An early record is “Thomas de Deware and Pieres de Dewere
of Edinburghshire rendered homage in 1296 ...”

Din. See Dun.

Variants of the surnmae Dunmore . The name is derived “From the old lands of Dundemore near
Lindores, Fife. The old family kept possession of the lands for a lengthened period, and took the
Scottish side in the Wars of Independence ... The family appears to have ended in the direct line
in an heir- female in the time of david II ...” An early record is “Henry de Dundemore witnessed a
confirmation charter by John, earl of Huntigdoun of land in Kynalchmund to the Abbey of
Arbroath c. 1219 ...”

“An old surname in Dumfriesshire, apparently a corruption of DURAND, ... Wautier Durand or
Durant who held land in Dumfriesshire in thirteenth century may have given name to the parish
of Kirkpatrick-Durand, later corrupted to Durham, the change probably influenced by Durham in
England.” An early record is John Dirrin in Kirkpatrick-Fleming, 1657 ...”

A variant of the surname Dishington. “The surname of a family prominent first in Angus and
afterwards in the East Neuk of Fife from the early fourteenth century to the sixteenth century.
Through intermarriage the Dishingtons became connected with many prominent Scottish
families. The name appears to be derived from Dissington in Northumberland, in OE. Dicing(a)-
t•n, the farm or tun of *Dica or his sons. The name is often familiarly contracted (in
pronunciation) to Distin.” “The first of the name recorded in Scotland appears to be Sir William
de Dissingtoun who received from Robert I a charter of the lands of Balglassy in the
thanedom of Abirlemenache in Angus ...”

Variants of the surname Dobbie. “The tradition that the first of this name in Scotland came from
France in the time of Mary Queen of Scots and that the name is Scotticized from De Bois is
erroneous. The surname, which is simply from Dobb, a pet form of Robert, with the diminutive
suffix - ie, existed in Scotland long before the time of Queen Mary.” An early record is “Thomas
Doby, younger, burgess of Peblis, son of Thomas Doby, elder, resigned the feu of his land in
1471 ...”

“ ‘Dog, Dogg, Doig, the surname of several landed families in the Kilmadok district, is for Gille
Dog, ‘St. Cadoc’s servant.’ ‘From Doc, Dog, Dogg, Doge, Doig, now Doig, Doag, Doak, a
surname which appears often on record, almost always in the neighbourhood of ... places in
which [St.] Cadoc was commemorated ...’ “ An early record is “Alexander Dog was canon of
Inchmahome in Menteith in 1491, when he resigned his lands of Auchounbannow to his brother
James.”

disappeared [etc., etc.] ... the name was written Domnall although sounded Dovnall’ ...” An early
record is “The contribution of Haket donald for peace was paid to the bailie of Kinross in 1328

Variants of the surname Dougal. “The OIr. form of the name is Dubgall, ‘black stranger,’ a
‘Dane.’ With ‘Mac’ we have MACDOUAL and MACDOUGAL, ... Dufgal occurs on a runic
stone in the Isle of Man as Tufcal, and in the form of Duggall it is found in Norse Konunga
Sögur ... Dufgal filius Mocche, ... appears in a complaint by the monks of St. Serf’s Island in
Loch Leven c. 1128 ... Reeves ... says this Dufgal ‘resembles the old Dubhgall of Scone who is
mentioned in the Irish tract on the men of Alba preserved in the Book of Ballymote and in
MacFirbis genealogic MS. ...’ The devocalization of - ll final suggested to the non-Gaelic ears
that a d or t followed, hence the spelling Dugald, and in caracature Tugalt.”

Dowell, James, auctioneer and appraiser, Hanover Street, B. and G. 29 Aug. 1839
“Of the Douglases, ‘the great, turbulent, daring, and too often treacherous house,’ as Lang calls
them ..., Hume of Godscroft the old historian of the family, writing of their origin says ‘We do
not know them in the Fountain but in the Stream; not in the Root, but in the Stock and Stem, for
we know not who was the first mean man that did raise ... himself above the vulgar’ ...” Black
then debunks several tales of the origin of the Douglas’. He continues “ ‘there is no proof nor
any probability of William of Douglas of the twelfth century, the undoubted ancestor of the
family, being descended of the Fleming who settled on the opposite side of his native valley’ ...”
An early record is “William de Duglas, the first of the family in record, between 1175 and 1199,
witnessed a confirmation charter by Jocelin, bishop of Glasgow to the monks of Kelso ...”

Variants of the surname Drummond. “The barony of Drummond was probably identical with
the parish of Drymen, of which name it is but a variant, the final d being excrescent. ‘Persons
deriving their designation from the lands of Drummond are frequent witnesses in the early
charters of the earls of Levenax; and the family appear to have held various lands in the earldom,
as well as offices in the household of the great earls of Levenax, at an early period and until they
migrated to the earldom of Stratherne’ ... The first of the name recorded is usually said to be
Malcolm, who witnessed charters by Maldouen, third earl of Levenax from 1225 to 1270. This
Malcolm was chamberlain to the earl and married Ada, his daughter.”

Variants of Deuchar. The name is “Of territorial origin from the lands of Deuchar in the lordship
of Fern or Fearn in Angus. The Deuchars of the Ilk were considered one of the oldest families in
the district, and are said to have come into possession of the lands of Deuchar about the year
1230. An imaginative genealogy ... traces the family to the second son of Gilchrist, earl of
Angus, but no documentary records of the family exist till 1369 when Sir alexander Lindsay of
Glenesk granted a charter of the lands of Deuhqwhyr to William Deuhqwhyr de eodem as heir to
his father ... The family were evidently vassals of the Lindsays at that period, and probably, at a
still earlier date, of the Montealtos (Mowats).

Variants of the surname Dun and Din. Black gives different origins for Dun and Din. Dynne is a
variant of Dun, but Din is not. Two origins are given for Dun: (1) of local or territorial origin,
perhaps from Dun in Angus. An early record is “Adam de Dun was elected to the deanery of
Moray in 1255 ...” (2) Celtic donn, ‘brown,’ was early naturilized in OE. as dunn, ‘dun,’ ‘dingy,’
or ‘brown,’ and became an OE. personal name, Dun, Dunna, Dunne. An early record is
“Malcolm, son of David Dunne of Conestablestoun, quitclaimed to the bishop of Glasgow the
lands of Tor or Windilawes in the territory of Edulfistune between 1260-68 ...” Din is “An old
Strathblane surname, frequent in Fintry in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.” An early
record is “William Din appears in Cardoroche, parish of Calder, 1627 ...”

Dunbarton, George, Earle of, B. and G., gratis 23 May 1685
„ George, Earl of, Commander- in-Chief of H.M. Forces in Scotland, gratis 4 June 1685

Derived from the “G. Donnchad, MG. (c. 1520) Duncha, and in the 1467 Gaelic genealogical
MS. it appears in the geitive as Donnchaid. The early Irish form Donnchad seems to represent
earlys Celtic Donno-catu-s, ‘brown warrior,’ from donn and cath. On an ogham stone at Glan
Usk near Crickhowel in Wales the name occurs spelled Dunocatus, which points to ‘fort
warrior,’ from dun, ‘fort,’ as the meaning of the name. The exact meaning is therefore
uncertain.” An early record is “Dunchad, eleventh abbot of Hii (Iona) died in 717 ...”

“The Dundases are certainly one of the oldest historical Scottish families in existence, though the
dates of the first of the name given in the above work [Dundas of Dundas] are placed too early.
Helias, son of Uctred or Huctred, who obtained the charter of the lands of Dundas in West
Lothian from Waldeve, son of Gospatric, most probably in the reign of Malcom IV or a little
later is first of the name recorded.”

“A well known Ayrshire surname derived from the lands of Dunlop in the district of
Cunningham. About the middle of last century the name was locally pronounced Delap or Dulap.
The first record of the surname appears to be in 1260 in which year dominus Willelmus de
Dunlop is recorded as witness to an indenture between Godfrey de Ross and the burgesses of
Irvine ...”

in glasgow in 1550 ...” “The Edmondstons take their name from Edmonstone, the tun of
Eadmund, near Edinburgh, their original home. The t•n may have derived its name from
Aedmund filius Forn, one of the witnesses to a charter by Thor filius Swani, c. 1150 ...”

A variant of the surname Ego. “A common surname in Braemar and Cromar in the seventeenth
century and earlier, and still found there. The name represents a Gaelic attempt at the name
Adam (Adhamh), with medial dh hardened to g. In the phonetically spelled Fernaig MS. (of date
1688) the name is written ‘Ahu,’ and in the still earlier manuscript of the Dean of Lismore (c.
1520) it appears as ‘Awzoe’ (z here a gutteral y).” An early record is “Eggou ruffus made a gift
of land to the Priory of May early in the thirteenth century ...”
Eggo, John, mt., Leith, B., in r. of w. Elizabeth, dr. of Robert Wilson, shoemaker ; also G.
  24 Dec. 1818

Eglunstone, had a grant of twenty acres of land in feuferme from the burgh of Irvine in 1205 ...”

Variants of the surname Elliot. “The early form of this well-known Border name was Elwald or
Elwold, for the full OE. (Old English) AElfwald, and until the end of the fifteenth century the
spelling of the name was fairly regular. … ‘Elwald’ as a Christian name became extinct, but
survived as a surname.”

Variants of the surname s Howden and Haldane . Very mixed up. Hadden and Haddon are
variants of the surname Howden, which in turn was derived from the old barony of Hadden or
Halden. Haldane has at least two origins, one Norse (Healfdene), and the other from “… a
younger son of the Border house of Hadden or Hauden …”

A variant of HALDAWACH. According to Black, the surname Haddo came from Alanus De
Haldawach who derived his name from Haddo in the parish of Forgue, Aberdeenshire and is
distinct from the Haddow below.

Variants of the surname Lumsden. Lumsdale is derived “From an old pronunciation and spelling
of LUMSDEN, q.v., which has become a fixed surname.” An early record of Lumsdale is “John
Lummisdaill was tacksman of 1½d land in Trymland, Orkney, in 1503 ...” Lumsden is derived
“From the old manor of that name in the parish of Coldingham, Berwickshire. The earliest
record of the name is between 1166-82, when Gillem (i.e. William) and Cren de Lumisden
witnessed a charter by Earl Waldeve of Dunbar to the Priory of Coldingham ...”
Lum[i]sden (Lumsdaill), Andw., B., F.C. 11 Feb. 1551-2

M’Gilrey in Dumfries-shire in 1376.

Variants of the surname Morrison. The name means son of Maurice or Morris. The name
Maurice [Morris], after a saint martyred in 286 A. D., was introduced into Britain by the
Normans.

A variant of Muter which is a form of the surname Multrar. “A multurer was one who ground
or had grain ground at a particular mill, [or] tacksman [tax man] of a mill.”

Myllar. See Miller.

Variants of the surname Miln and Mill. Black states that Mill is “A corruption for ease of
pronunciation of Miln or Milne.” Miln/Milne/Mylne is “Of local origin from residence at or near
a corn-mill.”

Scotland, godson of David I, acquired from the king lands in Roxburghshire, probably after
1141, ...”

“Paganus was a favorite personal name among the Normans (e.g. Paganus de Brausa, ...) and in
French was reduced to Payen and Pain and Paine. It is also a pre-Conquest name in England,
Ralph Pagan occurring in a document of 1055. The word ‘originally dnoted the inhabitant of a
pagus or country district. As such people were late in receiving new ideas, the modern notion of
pagan developed out of the word.”

Patullo. See Pittillo.

“This surname is one of considerable antiquity in the parish of Daviot, and occurs in the parish of
Fintry in 1654. It is also found in the Lothians and in Fife, where it is considered ‘by family
tradition a Flemish name’ ... , bit is not necessarily so.”

“From the office of porter, doorkeeper, or janitor of a castle or monastery. The porter was one of
the most important officials connected with the castle or monastic institutions. Lands and
privileges were attached to the office, and in the case of a roya l castle the position was often
hereditary …”

“In several monasteries, a portion of land was appropriated to the Porter. At Paisley this office
and land seems to have got into the hands of laymen, and to have become hereditary. The
descendeants of ‘John the Porter,’ inheriting the ‘porterfield’ naturally took the surname of their
office.”

Variants of the surname Provan. Derived “From the lands of Provan, formerly a possession of
the prebendary [A prebendary is property (or tithe) that provides a stipend for clergy]of
Barlanark, one of the canons of Glosgow cathedral. Provand is the vernacular for prebenda. A
surname around Glasgow and also surname of a family long connected with Strathblane and
Killearn.” Early records of the name occur in 1190, 1200 and 1231 for Richard de Prebenda.
Provan (Proven), Robert, cooper in Leith, B. and G., at the desire of Alexr. Swinton, clerk of
  the Canongate, for good services done by said Alexr. in attending the two general Conventions
  of Royal Borrowes held in Glasgow, gratis, by act of C. of 23 Aug. at the desire of the
  magistrates 18 Oct. 1704

Variants of the surname RANDALL. Randall is “An apocopated [apocope = loss or omission of
the last letter, syllable or part of a word] form of OE. [Old English] Randwulf or Randulf, from
Röndulfr, ‘shield wolf,’ a common ON. [Old Norse] personal name.”

Variants of the surname Ranald. Also, see Ronald. Derived from “The Anglicized form of G.
[Gaelic] Raonull, itself a borrowing from ON. [Old Norse] Rögnvaldr, ‘ruler of (from) the gods’
or ‘ruler of counsel.’ There are many early forms of spelling and pronunciation of this name,
e.g., Raghnall (1467), Ragnall, Rynilt, Rawnald, etc.

Variants of the surname Reekie. It is possible that Rikie and Riki are variants. The name “... may
be a diminutive of Rickart, q.v., a variant of Richard, and it may also be noted that there is a
place named Reikie in the parish of Alford, Aberdeeenshire.” An early record of the name is
John Rekie in Leith in 1567.

Derived “From Renton in the parish of Coldingham, Berwickshire, the ‘tun’ or town of Raegen
or Rein, a shortened form of the OE. [Old English] personal name Raegenweald. The Rentons of
Renton were hereditary foresters of Coldingham in the reign of William the Lion, and Ricardus
forestarius appears in record as Ricardus de Reningtona.”

Beware! There are at least two entries in this section that may apply only to the surname Liddell,
the last entry and the one for 20 Dec. 1721. The remaining entries are a mixture of variants are
derived from two distinct families. “The Ridels came from Gascony and the de Rydales from the
wapentake [a subdivision of a county or a law court in a county] of Ryedale in the North Riding
of Yorkshire. The two [names] appear almost simultaneously in Scotland, and the names are
always distinguished in spelling ... The Ridels never prefixed de, and the de Rydales invariably
did so ...”

Variants of the surname ROBERTON. “Of territorial origin from the manor of the same name,
now the parish of Roberton, Lanarkshire. In the reign of Malcolm IV the manor belonged to
Robert (the brother of Lambin who gave name to Lamington), and took its name from him.” An
early record is “Robert of Robertstun witnessed a charter by Hugh, son of Robert, son of
Waldeve de Bigar, granted at Lesmahago in 1296 ...”

Caution! At least in the first group of entries it appears that the editors comingled at least
Robertson and Robeson which are distinct surnames according to Black.. The name, Robertson,
means son of Robert. An early record of the name is “William Robertson (fils [son of] Robert), a
Scot going abroad, had English letters of protection in 1371 ...”

The name is a dimunutive of Robert. An early record is “Mareoun Robyn was a tenant in Stobo
in 1540 ...”
Robin, Mr. Henry, minr., B. and G., be r. of w. Agnes, dr. to dec. Mr. David Williamson, minr.
  at St. Cuthbert’s 5 Apr. 1721

Perhaps = son of Robin.
Robins , George, B. and G., Esqr., gratis, at the request of the Lord Chancellor Desburrow
 (Desborough) 6 Aug. 1658

The name means “The ‘son of Robert’ from Robin, a diminutive form of the name. ... [In one
record] the same individual is referred to as Robyne of Hall and Robert of Hall.” An early record
is “The tenement of John Robynson in Irvine is mentioned in 1426 ... “

Rosewell, Mr. James, minr. of the gospel at London, B. and G., gratis 11 Sept. 1706

There are at least two origins for the surname. “(1) The first record of this surname in Scotland is
in Ayrshire, a considerable portion of the northern part of which in the twelfth century was held
by a family of Ros or Ross, that came from Yorkshire.” “(2) In the north the surname is derived
from the district of Ross. Malcolm, earl of Ross, c. 1150, was of the Gaelic family of O’Beolán.
‘There never was an earl who bore the surname of Ross, but when the title passed to descendants
in the female line, the lairds of Balnagown assumed the name as male representatives of the
earls.’ “ See Rose above, since some Roses are included with the Ross’.

Variants of the surname Shand. “A rare but old surname in Scotland. ‘The surname of Shand
seems originally to have been confined to the north-eastern counties, particularly Aberdeenshire,
and in that county more especially to the districst comprising the parishes of Turriff, Forgue,
Drumblade, Auchterless, Culsalmond, Fyvie, King- Edward and Gamrie. In old times it was
variously spelled Schawand, Schaand [etc.]..., ‘ “ An early record is Magister Robert Schawnd
was prebendary [a person receiving revenue from a church property or tithe; sometimes an
honorary title] of Arnaldston, 1522 ... “

Variants of the surname Shannan. The name is derived from the “Ir. [Irish] O’Seanáin,
diminutive of sean, old, wise. In Galloway and Kintyre the name was formerly current as
Aschennan.” An early Scottish record is “Dungall Achinyane in Wigtownshire, was retoured heir
of Cuthbert Aschennane of Park, killed at Pinkiecleuch, 1548...”

Variants of the surname Shaw. There are at least two origins to the surname. (1) The Lowland
surname of Shaw is of territorial origin. ... The families of this name, of south country origin, are
found mainly in Kirkcudbrightshire, Ayrshire, around Greeock, and in Stirlingshire.” An early
record of this branch is “John de Schau witnessed the resignation of the lands of Aldhus to the
monks of Paisley in 1284 ... “”(2) Norther Shaw (of Aberdeenshire, a branch of Clan Chattan)
has nothing to do with Lowland Shaw. Shaw was adopted as being that most nearly resembling
the Gaelic na me in pronunciation. The first record of the name is in one of the Gaelic entries in
the Book of Deer, recording ‘Donnachac mac Sithig toesech clenni Morgainn’ (Duncan mac
Sithech, toisech of Clan Morgan), ... “

Variants of the surname Sinclair. “This Caithness surname is of territorial origin from St. clare
in the arrondissement [a municipal subdivision] of Pont d’Eveque, Normandy. The first Sinclairs
in Scotla nd appear to have been vassals of the great territorial magnates, de Morville. Their first
possession in Scotland was the barony of Roslin, near Edinburgh, ... 1124 ... The sinclairs, like
the Gordons and some other families, cannot be called a clan in the true sense of the term. They
were a powerful territorial family, whose relationship to their dependents was entirely feudal.”
An early record is “John Singular held land in Aberdeen, c. 1450 ...”

and it is possible that the name is of English origine, as many of the burgesses of the town in the
thirteenth century were of English nationality. It may be mentioned, however, that there are
local place names from which the surname may have come.”

Variants of the surnames Smalley and Smellie. Caution! It appears that, at least in the first two
groups of entries, two distinct surnames have been mixed. Smalley is perhaps of territorial
origin. “There is a Smalley in Derbyshire. In regards to the origin of Smellie, “Harrison derives
the name as a variant of Smalley, from the name of a place in Derbyshire, but I [Black] feel
doubtful of this.” An early record of Smalley is “A deed of 1283 runs in the name of ‘Oliverus et
Ricardus Smally ...” An early Smellie record is “Thomas smelie, merchant and guildbrother
in Glasgow, 1612 ...”

Variants of the surname Symmers . Derived from “... Somer, a sumpter [perhaps involved with
water pits in mines or salt works], applied to both men and horses [a pack horse], OF. [Old
French] somier, sommier.” An early record is “William Sumer witnessed a grant by Richard de
Paynstoun to the Hospital of soltre between 1180-1214 ...”

Variants of the surname Somerville. Derived “From a town near Caen in Normandy, Sumar’s or
Somer’s estate.” “William de Somerville, first of the name in Scotland, came in the train of
David I, and received lands in Lanarkshire.”

Variants of the surname Spittal. Derived from “ME. [Middle English] spital, an aphetised
[shortened by losing a syllable which is short and unaccented] form of OFr. [Old French]
hospital. The old Dumbartonshire family of Spittal derived their name from the lands of Spittal
in the parish of Kilmaron, which at an earlier date had belonged to the Knights Hospitallers ...”
An early record is “In or before 1394 Adam de spydeloch resigned the lands of Ladlewn ...
Walter de Spetalle alias Walterus de Hospitali, received from David II a charter ... 1365 ... “

Variants of the surname Sproat. The name is “Perhaps from Sprot, an OE. [Old English]
personal name, but more likely to be of Scandinavian origin ... The tradition of those bearing this
name in Scotland is that their ancestors were Saxons who came into Scotland after the Norman
Conquest of England.” “The first recorded of the name in Scotland appears to be Hugh Sprot of
Ur who witnessed a charter ... in 1262...”

name in the parish of Larbert, Stirlingshire.” Stanhope , on the other hand is “A surname most
probably assumed from Stanhope in Tweeddale, but it does not appear that those lands ever were
possessed by persons of the name ...”

The origin of the name is uncertain. “Burke (Landed gentry) says the family of Stark claims
descent from Alexander Robertson of Strowan who died 1506 or 1507. Tradition relates that
Alexander, younger son of Paul Robertson, having taken part in the family feuds of the day (who
at that time did not?), was found guilty of manslaughter and fled to the Lowlands where he
acquired the lands of Ballindean, having changed his name to Stirk or Stark.” An early record is
“William Stark was tenant in Castalstaris in 1540 ...”

Variants of the surnames Stephen and Steven. Origin of Stephen: “This name was introduced
into Britain by the Normans, with whom it was a favorite.Although found occasionally in
England before 1066, its use then was due really to Christion tradition, Stephen (Stephanos)
having been the first Christian martyr after Christ. Origin of Steven: “A Scots spelling of
Stephen, ...” Two early records: “Stephen, diaconus [the deacon], witnessed a charter by Bishop
Edward, c. 1150-71 ...” “Alexander Stevyn was tenant of Glenboy in 1472 ...”
