Variants of the surname Stewart. “In OE. [Old English] the original sense of the word stiward ...
was one who looked after the domestic animals; hence by extension of meaning, one who
provides for his master’s table. By the eleventh century the word had come to mean one who
superintended the housefold affairs of another, and was therfore a title of honor. In Scotland the
steward was not only chief of the royal household, but his power extended to the collection and
management of the crown revenues, to the administration of justice, and in time of war he took
first place in the army next to the king.” “The Scottish royal family of Stewart descended from a
family of Breton nobles, who were hereditary seneschals of Dol. The first recorded is Alan
Dapifer [Dolensis], who flourished about the middle of the eleventh century. ... Walter, [a
descendant of Alan] was the first of his family in Scotland. He first appears in 1142 ... King
David before his death in 1153 made a grant to this Walter of the office of Steward of Scotland.
... Robert II [a descendant of Walter’s], [was] first of the royal line of Stewart, crowned in 1371.
“ There are many Stewart lines, not all are descended from royalty. “Every bishop, every earl
had his steward, who in his own particular domain was simply ‘John the steward.’ “ A non-royal
early record is “Phelippe Styward of Roxburghshire and William le fiz le Stywarde of the counte
of Berewyk rendered homage, 1296 ...”

Variants of the surname Stoddard. Derived “From the office of ‘stot- hird,’ one who tended the
stots, i.e. bullocks.” “The earliest mention of this surname in Scotland is in 1376 when David
Stodhirde, John Studehird, and William Studhirde are recorded as tenants of Douglas in barony
of Buittle ...”

Variants of the surname Struthers . Derived from “The ME. [Middle English] element strother, a
marsh or swamp. ... There is a Struther near Stonehouse, Lanarkshire, and a Struthers in Fife, but
the references point to an origin further south, perhaps from Strother in Northumberland. The
ancient Northumberland family of Strothers were lords of the maonor of Kirk-Newton in the
barony of Wark on the Tweed.” An early record is “John Strwtheris was witness in Glosgow,
1555 ...”

Variants of the surname Symington. “The re is a village and parish of Symington in the Kyle
district of Ayrshire, but the old family of Symington derive from Symington in the Upper Ward
of Lanarkshire. Symon Loccard, ancestor of the Lockharts of Lee, held both places in the latter
half of the twelfth century under the Stewards. Between 1315-21 Robert I confirmed to Thomas
filius [son of] Ricardi all the barony of Symundestone in the sheriffdom of Lanark ... This
Thomas son of Richard (Thomas Dickson) was progentior of the family of Symington of that
Ilk.” An early record is “John of Symonton of that Ilk appears as sheriff-depute of Lanark in
1478 and 1490 ...”

Tabet, Charles, Esq., B. and G., gratis, by act of C. 25 June 1729

Variants of the surname Telfer. Derived “From NF. [Norman French] taillefer, ‘cut iron,’
perhaps a trade name [Taillefer , fl. 1066, Norman warrior and trouvère. According to medieval
chronicles and evidence in the Bayeux Tapestry, he led the Norman army at Hastings into battle,
singing of Roland at Roncesvalles; he was killed in the conflict.].” An early record is “Willelmus
Tailfer witnessed a charter by Margaret, countess of Buchan, in favor of the Abbey of Arbroath,
c. 1210 ...”

Tain, John, B., mt. (corslet), as eldest s. to umq. Patrick T., B. 31 May 1643

The surname was “Originally a nickname. ... Ethelberga, daughter of Ethelbert, king of Kent,
was otherwise called ‘Tate’ (fem.) and nine individuals named ‘Tata’ (masc.) are recorded ... The
word meaning ‘glad,’ ‘cheerful,’ occurs in ON. [Old Norse] as teitr, and as a proper name, Teitr,
occurs several times in the Icelandic Landnúmabok.” An early record is “A debt due by the king
is recorded paid to Thomas dictus [to say] Tayt in 1329 ...”

“From the village of Temple in the parish of the same name in Midlothian, formerly the principal
place of residence of the Knights Templars in Scotland. ‘The preceptories or priories of Knights-
Templars were often called Temples, and even manorial residences and estates blonging to them
obtained the same appellation. The name consequently passed to tenant or bailiff of such a
property.”

“A common Anglo-Norman personal name. It is from the Syriac te’oma, Hebr. to’am, ‘twin,’
rendered by Greek Didymus in St. John, XI: 16. In Gaelic it assume the forms Tomas, Tamhus,
hence the Gaelick patronymics MACTAVISH, MACCOMBIE, and MACOMIE, q.v. As a
surname in Scotland it is of late introduction from England.”

   deficultie for the tyme, And sieing sensyn he has spurnd at the bussines and will have his owen
   privat way of transactioun beside by the rest of the nighbors, And hes his owen indirect weyis

   therof Dischairges the said James Thomsone from the exercise of his calling as a Frieman
   burges or gild brother of this Brugh In tyme comeing And ordaines his burges ticket to be riven
   And his act of admissioun to be deleitt And to abyd farder censure at the discretioun of the

Variants of the surname Toschach. = “ ‘chief,’ ‘leader,’ or ‘front man.’ An ancient Gaelick
dignity ranking next to the mormaer. The word is found on a Welsh ogham- inscribed stone as
tovisaci, in Welsh tywysog, and on several of the early British coins it appears under the Latin
form of Tascio.”

Derived “From OF. [Old French] trotier, mod. Fr. trotteur, a runner, messenger. There was a

Variants of the surname TURING. “An Aberdeenshire surname first found in 1323 in the
person of Adam Turin, who is mentioned in a deed regarding the park of Fyvin ... The family
was originally of Norman origin, and is said to have first settled in Angus in a barony of the
same name, moving from there to Aberdeenshire about beginning of fourteenth century. ”

of Fulhopalche (now Philiphaugh) to William called Turnebule (Whllelmo dicto turnebule) ...”

A variant of the surname OCHILTREE. “A race of MacUchtres who held lands in Glendaruel

Black lists Edard/Udwart as distinct from Edward/Edwart, BUT .... UDARD/UDWART were
derived “From Udard-us, an OE. [Old English] personal name ... Udward or Udwart was an old
surname occuring frequently in the sixteenth century, but was later lost in EDWARD ...”
EDWARD was derived “From the OE. [Old English] personal name Eadweard, ‘happy ward’ or
‘guardian’ ... The name was early confused with UDARD, ... and Peter ... says the old name of
the family of Edward of Balruddery in Angus was Uduard.”

Derived “From the office of ‘doorkeeper,’ ME. [Middle English] uschere ... The office of the
usher was to keep the door of the king’s apartment and in addition he was required to know the
rank and precedence of all sorts of men, how they should be grouped at table, and many other
matters.” An early record is “Thomas the Usser mentioned in 1291 ... is referred to in the
following year as Thomas the Doorward.”

William the Lion a grant of the baronies of Panmure Bervie ...”

surname in England.”

Variants of the surname Waddel. Derived “From Wedale, the old name of the
parish of Stow in Midlothian.” “The earliest know bearer of the name is Adam de
Wedale, ‘an outlaw of the King of Scots land,’ who appears in 1204 ...”

Variants of the surname Walker. “A trade name from OE. [Old English] wealcere, ME. [Middle
English] walker, a fuller or thickener of woollen cloth, ...” An early record is “Thomas dictus
Walkar in record in Berwick in 1324 ...”

“From the lands of the same name in Renfrewshire. The Walkinshaws of that Ilk were
descended from Duugallus filius Cristini, judex de Levenax, who about 1235 made excambion of
his lands of Cnoc for the la nds of Walkeinschaw ... The Walkinshaws were hereditary foresters
to the High Stewards for the barony of Renfrew, ...”

Variants of the surname WALLACE. “Wallensis meant a Briton of Strathclyde as we see from
charters of the twelfth century to the people of the Glasgow diocese (extending from Clyde to
Solway) headed: Francis et Anglicis, Scotis et Galwiensibust et Walensibus, ‘to French and
English, Scots (coast of Ayrshire, tec.), Galloway men and Britons (of Strathclyde).’ Wallace is
therfore most probably a native name meaning a Strathclyde Briton.” An early record is “Richard
Wal[ensis] who attested a charter by Walter, son of Alan, between 1165-73 ... appears to be first
of the name recorded. As Richard Walency he (c. 1190) witnessed a charter by Richard de
Lincoln ...”

“A personal name, Teutonic Walther, Walthar, OE. [Old English] W(e)aldhere, ‘powerful
warrior.’ Wealdhere in AF. [Anglo-French] became Wautier, which when spelled Walter at a
later period was long pronounced Water, and so gave name to Wat, Watt, and Wattie.”

Variants of the surname Wardrop. Derived “From the office of the keeper of the royal
wardrobe. The wardrobe was a repository not only for articles of dress, but for furniture not
actually in use, and for foreign spices and confections ...” An early record is “Robertus de
Warderob witnessed a charter by Margaret, countess of Buchan in favor of the Abbey of
Arbroath, c. 1210 ...”

Variants of the surname Weston. A local surname. “There are places named Weston and
Westoun in Lanarkshire, and a Weston near Dolphinston, Peeblesshire.” An early record is
“William de Westone of Wyggetone rendered homage in 1296.”

Variants of the surname WATSON. Derived from “ ‘son of Walter,’ from the diminutive form
Wat or Watt.” An early record is “Sir Donaldus Walteri, a prebyter of the diocese of Moray,
1493, is mentioned in a document of 1612 as Sir Donald Watsone ...”

Variants of the surname Waterson. “A surname of territorial origin from more than one place of
the name. (1) From lands of the name formerly in the parish of Fearn. These lands probably
obtained their name from Walter, uncle and tutor of Dempster, one of the heirs portioners of the
lordship of Menmuir. ... (2) In the reign of Robert II William Waterstoun of that Ilk alienated the
lands of Waterstoun in the parish of Kilbarchan, Renfrewshire, ... (3) There are also Watersons
of that Ilk in Midlothian.”

Variants of the surname Waugh. “The author of The House of Glendinning (p. 5) says: ‘The
common border name of Waugh is an abbrevieation of Wauchope, the Waughs are sprung from
the Wauchopes and have the same arms.’ “ An early record is “David de Waughe of Lanarkshire,
Robert Walgh’ de Hepe [from lands of Heip or Heap in the parish of Wilton] of Roxburghshire,
and Thomas Walghe of Peeblesshire rendered homage in 1296 ...”

Weill, James, G., mt., B. of before I Jan. 1600

The name is “Of Norman origin from one or other of the places named Vere in Calvados,
Manche, Eure-et-Loire, and Oise. The word was introduced into Normandy by the Norsemen
from their own ver, a station, as in fiskiver, a fishing station, a word etymologically akin to OE.
[Old English] weir, wear, a dam.” An early record is “Ralph or Radulphus de Ver is perhaps the
first of the name recorded in Scotland. As Ralph de Ver he was taken prisoner at Alnwick along
with William the Lion in 1174 ...”

in Fife.” “The surname Methkil is [see below] derived from the lands of the same name, now
Methil in Fife.” An early record is “The first known of the name was Michael de Methkil (q.v.)
who was variously called by that or by that of de Wemys.” “John de Methkil granted the church
of Wemyss in Fife to the House of Soltre sometime between 1200 and 1240 ...”

Variants of the surname Whytoch. The name is “Perhaps of local origin from Whitehauch,
anciently Quhithauch, in Liddesdale. There is, however, an OE. [Old English] personal name,
Hwittuc or Hwituc, from which it may be derived.” An early record is “Whilliam Quhittok in
Edinburgh had a precept of sasine in 1576 ...”

Variants of the surname Wyld. The surname is “Usually explained as ‘wild, untamed, violent,’
but more likely local from residence at a weald or open country. Bardsley says Wild ‘was a
popular sobriquet in Yorkshire judging by the 1379 Poll Tax and the present county directory.’
Yorkshire is well known for its Wolds and the Weald of Sussex is also called the Wild.” An
early record is “Philip Wilde, M.A., of the diocese of Brechin, was granted a canonry of
Glasgow in 1342 ...”

Variants of the surname Wilkie. “The name is a double diminutive of William, q.v.” William is
“From Old Germ.[an] Willihelm. The name [Willihelm/William]is found in 1317 ... Adam, the
Conqueror. For centruies in England it and John have raced for first place in popularity. It has
been the source of a vast number of surnames in Britain and on the continent, ...”

Variants of the surname Wilkieson. = “ ‘son of Wilkie,’ ...” Wilkenson is a variant of
Wilkinson, not Wilkieson. Wilkinson = “ ‘son of Wilkin,’ ... From this [Wilkinson] comes
MACQUILKAN, a name meth with in Kintyre.”

Variants of the surname Wotherspoon. “The meaning of this name is uncertain. ‘Sheep pasture,’
has been reasonably suggested from OE. [Old English] and ME. [Middle English] weoer, ‘sheep,
lamb,’ and spong, obsolete English for a tongueshaped piece of land enclosed by or lying next to
higher ground.” An early record is “ ‘Widderspune the foulare that tald talis and brocht foulis to
the king’ received a payment in 1496 ...”

Variants of the surname Wood. The name is “Local, from residence near a wood (OE. [Old
English] wudu). The name appears first in record in the Latinized form de Bosco (see Boyce).
There is an OE. personal name, Wuda, from which the name might be derived. This became in
ME. [Middle English] Wode, and later Wood, buth the local derivation is most probable for the
name in Scotland.” An early record is “William Wod was a witness to the valuation of Kilravock
and Easter Geddes in 1295 ...”

Variants of the surname Wright. Derived “... from OE. [Old English] wyrhta, a worker, chiefly
in wood, a carpenter. With Scots it has displaced Carpenter, a surname of Latin origin.” An early
record is “Rauf le Wrighte, burgess of Stirling, and Thomas le Whright of the Blakehalle of
Lanarkshire rendered homage in 1296 ...”

Variants of the surname Yates. The name is “Of local origin from one or more small places of
the name meaning ‘at the gate,’ from OE. [Old English] geat, ME. [Middle English] yate. ‘A
final s is not uncommon in surnames derived from topographical features, and may be either the
plural formation or genitive case ending, but it is not possible to say which from inspection,’ or,
again, it may be ‘a meaningless excressence, the addition of a terminal sibilant being not
uncommon with uncultured people’ ...” An early record is “Adam del Yate was juror on an
inquisition held at Lochmaben in 1347 ...”

A variant of the surname YEOMAN. “From ME. [Middle English] yoman, yeman, ?eman,
originally a countryman or retainer, but later a freeholder next under the rank of gentleman, a
man who owned tree land of forty shillings annual value. ... The surname is of comparative late
appearance in Scotland. George Zeman appears as tenant of the bishop of Moray in 1565 ...”

Variants of the surname YORSTOUN. “An old surname in the parish of Corstorphine,
Edinburgh, where a family of this name held the land to the east of the village known as
‘Yorkstounis.’ ... A family of the same name is early found in Orkney. ... The evidence ... points
strongly to Rowsay as their home, and is corroborated by later documents, and by the fact of an
early marriage with the Craigies of Brough ...”

The name is “A personal name the same in meaning with Gaelic Og, ‘young.’ The name was
probably applied, as Bardsley suggests, ‘in the sense of junior, to distinguish father and son when
both bore the same personal name.’ “ Two early records are “Malmor dictus Juvenis [younger,
junior] and Ade dictus Juvenis were assizers at Dumbarton in 1271 ... John Yong de Dyngvale
witnessed a charter by the earl of Ross to Reginald, son of Roderick of the Isles, in 1342 ...”

The name is “The comparative of Young, signifying the younger of two bearing the same
Christian name. In Latin documents redered Junior. [Black also cites two references but
doesn’t support or deny the suggestions: (1) That the name Younger [Joncker, Youncker]is of
Flemish origin and often associated with saltmaking. (2) ‘The name of Younger, it seems, is of
the same stock with the Youngs by their arms’ An early record is “William Yhunger was a
tenant of the Douglas in Telny in the barony of Abirdoure in Fife in 1376 ...”

Variants of the surname Yule. “The usual explanation of this name as ‘one given to children
born on Christmas day,’ does not satisfy me, but I am at present unable to offer a satisfactory
interpretation in place of it. ‘It is pretended that the Yuilles are descended of a son of Drumkills,
born upon Yuilday. This pretension is adhered to by some of the name Yuille, by others not ...’ “
An early record is “Johannes Yhole was burgess of Haddington in 1374 ...”

EXPLANATIONS, GLOSSARY, ETC., 1406 - 1700
A. Indicates a gentleman made burgess along with and at the desire of Gen.-Major Middleton,
  8 Jan. 1647.
Abbot of Na Rent. Seems to be the same as the Abbot of Unreason (see “The Abbot,” chap.
  xiv.). He is coupled with Robin Hood.
Adv. = Advocate.
Alias. Occurs fairly often, especially in “ alias Captain.” The following are instances :—
  John Hope, 14 March 1516-7.
  Hawl Mason.
  John Mason, 3 Dec. 1558.
  John Mason, 5 May 1574.
  James M’Gill, 27 June 1660.
  Archd. Paterson, anno 1494
  John Pennycoke,25 Sept. 1488.
  John Spottiswood, 9 Aug. 1620.
  John Strauchin, 29 Nov. 1488.
  George Todrig, 18 March 1540-1.
  Wm. Vanderbought, 22 July 1657.
  Thos. Wilson, 14 Sept. 1563.
Allutarius = tanner.
Apoth. = apothecary.
App. reg.= Register of apprentices.
Archbp. = Archbishop.
Archicoquus=head cook.
Arenarius==sand digger or vender.
Arragia= customary duties (?).
Aula=hall.
Aurifaber, aurifex=goldsmith.
B.=burgess.
Barbetonsor;= barber.
Baxter, bagster= baker.
Black litster= black dyer.
Bower =bowmaker.
Bp.=Bishop.
Brasener = brass-worker.
Brodinster, broudster= embroiderer.
Brouster == brewer.
But = without.
C.== Council (Town).
(C.)=by act of C. only, not in burgess register.
Caitchpeller = keeper of a caitchpell or tennis court.
Capilliciarius = periwigmaker.
Capo=caupo, taverner (?).
Cap seller, cop seller = seller of wooden bowls.
Carnifex=flesher.
Carpentarius = carpenter.
Cellarius= vintner, butler.
Cerarius= wax-worker or chandler.
C.I. Refers to the visit of Charles I. to Edinburgh, August 1641. His household staff were
  admitted, the nobles and gentlemen as B. and G., the rank and file as B., among whom were
  :—
  Y.=Yeoman of the Guard.
  f.==H.M. futeman.
  G.=H.M. groom of the great horses.
  M.== Messenger of H.M. chalmier.
  All gratis.
C.I. Banquet. Indicates admission gratis by act of council at the banquet given to Charles I.,
  23 June 1633, in presence of the provost, bailies, dean of guild, thesaurer, and part of the guild
  council.
Chairman = porter of a (sedan) chair.
Cheirothecus= glover.
Chir.=chirurgeon, surgeon.
Claith-drapper= cloth-draper.
Claviger=macer.
Clericus= clerk.
Cocquetour=cook.
Condicillus=codicil, list.
Copseller. See capseller.
Coquus ==cook.
Conarius= tanner.
(Corslet) = furnished with a corslet, needed for admission as a guild-brother.
Cramer= occupant of a crame, or booth.
Cubicularius = “chamber chyld,” valet.
Culina=kitchen.
Cultellarius, cultellar=cutler.
Customarye=levying of customs or excise.
Customer=receiver of customs or excise.
D. of A. & Y. Indicates that the burgess admitted is one of the train of the Duke of Albany and
  York, afterwards James VII., who was made burgess and guild-brother along with his train,
  26 Dec. 1679.
D.C.S.D.H.=according to list given in to the Lord Provost by David Crawfurd, Secretary to the
  Duke of Hamilton, of his servitors and others.
d.= died.
Dagmaker== pistol maker..
Darien Scheme. The following names appear connected therewith.
  Alexr. Hamilton, 17 May 1699.
  Lieut. James Ker.
  Major John Lindsay.
  Capt. Daniel M’Kay, 30 Aug. 1699.
  Michael Sheills, 26 July 1699.
  Capt. Wm. Veitch, 26 July 1699.
Dewtie=fee.
Dominus, clerical title. With “miles”= Sir ... Kt.
Dr. “daughter.
Eld.=elder, eldest.
Epphipiarius = saddler.
Extents = assessments.
F.= freeman.
f. See Charles I.
F.C. Indicates that the duty was paid for the “ Fabric of the Church “ (St. Giles). John Wilson
   paid 11 April 1561 “to the reperralling (repairing) of the Kirk,” and Arthur Hamilton, the same
   day, “to the Kirk wark.” (See also act of 27 March 1568.) The last such entry seems to be
   John Craig, lorimer, 19 May 1561.
Faber= craftsman.
„ ferrarius= blacksmith.
,, lignarius=wright.
„. muriarius = builder, mason.
Fear=one to whom property belongs in reversion.
Fermorar= farmer.
Ferrier=farrier.
Foderator = furrier.
Fossor= grave digger
Fr.=father.
Fructuarius= fruit seller.
Fullo= fuller, waulker.
G. = guild-brother.
G.fr. == grandfather.
Gallearius = sailor.
Gemmarius = jeweller.
Gnall.= General.
(Hagbuit)==Armed with a hagbut or arquebus. (See act of 24 Dec. 1567.)
Hr. appt.= heir apparent.
Hekil=heckling comb.
Imbrodinster= embroiderer.
lndweller=resident in Edinburgh, unless otherwise stated.
Institor== pedlar, cramer.
Jack, jak=coat of mail.
Javelor= jailor.
Knock = clock.
Lanio=flesher.
Lathamus, lathomus, latomus = quarryman, mason.
Legged dollar. Jameson gives “perhaps a dollar of Liege.” Another derivation is from a Dutch
   coin, in which an armed man seems to have but one leg, the other being hidden by his shield.
   They are mentioned from about 1689 to 1694 or so. Legged dollars :—
   Jas. Goodwin.
   John Halliday, 21 Aug. 1689.
   Geo. Lapslie, 12 Dec. 1694.
   David Miller, 20 Jan. 1693.
  James Rule, 10 May 1693.
  James Young, 17 Oct. 1694.
  John Strauchan, 8 April 1691.
  James Thomson, 26 April 1693.
  Joseph Thomson, 23 Sept. 1692.
Lichnopeus=candlemaker.
Litster, littister=dyer.
M. See Charles I.
M.B.=merchant burgess; see 8 Dec. 1500.
M. 1500= burgesses made between 2 March 1498-9 and Michaelmas 1500. These are entered in
  one lot.
M.T.C.=minutes of Town Council.
Marikin maker = maker of dressed goat’s skin or Spanish leather.
Masser=macer.
Mercator= merchant.
Messr.—messenger.
Metstar= official measurer.
Minr.= minister.
Mr. =magister, a teacher or employer, or one who has a college degree equivale nt to M.A.
(Muskitt) = armed with a musket. The rule of “that anyone being made burgess must be
  sufficiently airmit with ane furnisht muskitt” began after 3 Nov. 1591, and the last man so
  appearing was Thos. Dods, plumber, 31 Jan. 1644.
Na-Rent. See Abbot of Na-Rent.
Nick names and Trade names occur occasionally, e.g. John Reid (17 April 1562] or Fat John.
  Robert Daniel, gardener to Mr. Cant, is entered burgess as Daniell Gairdner (23 June 1680).
  John Hope (14 March 1516-17) appears also as “ Petit Johne.”
Oy, Oye, Oe= grandchild.
P.==’prentice (prenteis).
P.R.=from the Printed Records of Edinburgh. (ScottishBurgh Records Society, 1869.)
Paenarium == pantry.
Paitlet, paytellat=a woman’s ruff.
Panton heel maker, maker of heels for slippers.
Pattesier=pastry cook.
Pellio= bonnet maker.
Pelliparius= furrier.
Pilearius, pileator==hat maker.
Piscarius== fishmonger.
Pistor=baxter, baker.
Plegius=surety, cautioner.
pnt.= present.
Potticar, pottefar==apothecary.
Pretorium=Tolbooth.
Procr. = procurator.
Pultreman = poultryman.
Quheilwright = wheelwright.
Quondam =umquhyle, late, deceased.
Note.—Quh is usual where wh is now used.
r.= right. be r. of = by right of.
Regent=schoolmaster or professor.
Residence. When a man was made a burgess of Edinburgh who was not an “indweller,” it was on
  the condition “that he sail come and make his residence within this burgh betwix [now] and
  Mertimes (or Witsonday) nixtocum,” often under the surety of a friend, and the risk of “ tynseil
  of his fredome,” or a fine of 100 pounds (Scots) in the event of failure.
Robin Hood. Robertus Hud or Huid. The citizen playing this character seems to have had the
  right to admit a burgess gratis. For the riot which broke out in 1561 when the magistrates
  attempted to suppress the Saturnalia, the games of Robin Hood, See Knox, “ History of the
  Reformation in Scotland.”
s.=son.
s. and h.=son and heir.
s. and h. appt. = son and heir apparent.
S.H.M.C.H.=servantto His Majesty’s High Commissioner, admitted gratis 9 Oct. 1696.
Saltare=salter, maker of salt.
Sarcinator = patcher (?), sackmaker (?).
Sartor == tailor.
Scissor=tailor.
Sledder= driver of a sled or sledge, much used over soft ground in preference to
wheeled carts.
Souertie= surety or cautioner.
Spargener= plasterer.
Sphaeristerium= bowling green.
Spices and wine. In very early days instead of paying in money for admission, the new burgess
  furnished “spices and wine” as a treat to those admitting him.
Stallarius= stabler.
Stob and staik= permanent residence.
Sumlier= butler (sommelier).
Sutor=cordiner, shoemaker.
Swerde-slipper= sword sharpener.
Tacksman (taxman)== tenant, holding the lease or “ tack.”
Tan nator= tanner.
Tegularius= tiler, slater.
Textor = weaver.
Tinctor=litster, dyer.
Tinsel, tynseil =loss.
Tonsor = barber.
Tubinnator= trumpeter.
umq.=umquhyle, late, deceased.
Upset=fee for entering-as ‘prentice.
Vestiarius = clothier.
Vitri compositor = glassinwright, glazier.
w.=wife. Conjux, uxor( and most frequent, sponsa. Be r. of w.= by right of his
wife (daughter to a burgess).
Warit= expended.
Walker, waker=waulker, fuller.
Weyver, wobster= weaver.
Women burgesses. A wife could transmit to her husband the right of admission coming from her
  father as a burgess, but women were themselves eligible, although the instances are very rare
  of their being made burgesses. For examples see :—
  Alison Duscoul, 17 March 1406-7.
  Ann Keith, 28 April 1665.
  Agnes Alison, 13 June 1683.
  Also Margaret Gray, under Thos. Brown, 3 Aug. 1642.
In the note of fees, 1 Dec. 1450 (q.v.), the feminine form “ post natae” seems to indicate that the
  right was claimed and exercised.

ABBREVIATIONS, &c [1761 - 1841].
Act of C. = Act of Council.
B. = burgess of Edinburgh.
By, or in, r. of=by, or in, right of.
Creamer = occupant of a cream or kraim (booth).
D.G. = Dean of Gild.
Dr. = daughter.
Fr.= father.
G. = gild brother.
H.E.I.C.S. = Honble. East India Company.
Indweller = resident [in Edinburgh].
In r. of=in or by right of.
Mt. = merchant.
M.T.C. = Minutes of Town Council.
Orris [and livery lace weaver]. A peculiar kind of gold or silver lace ; upholsterer’s galloon and
  gimp.
P. = apprentice.
R.N. = Royal Navy.
Reedmaker = maker of “reeds” for weavers.
Residenter = inhabitant [of Edinburgh].
Running stationers, or “cadies” who were stationed to run errands.
S. = son.
Sen. Coll. Just. = Senator of the College of Justice.
Surg.-apoth.= surgeon-apothecary.
Tronman= chimney sweep. They kept their brushes, &c. in a shed at the east end of the Town
  Guard, close to the “Salt
Tron,” or beam and scales, from which the Tron Church takes its name.
W. = wife.
When anyone is admitted “ by act of C.” and no date given, the date of the act is the same as that
  of the entry. When no qualification for burgess-ship is given, the admission was granted on
  payment of dues, exigible from unfreemen.
The barbers had a curious fashion of being “freeman Burgess Barber” (David Lawrie, P.
  9/4/1777). The tailors similarly, and often, “member of the Incorporation of Taylors of
  Edinburgh.”
When two brothers are in a firm, the surname is entered in plural form. Thus, George Miller, mt.,
  is made B. and G. 16 Nov. 1771 as p. to William and Thomas Tods, mts., B. and G.
ACT OF COUNCIL, 1701 - 1760.
15 Dec. 1615.—“The same (day; the counsell haveing consideratioune and respect to the guid
service done to thame and thair predecessors be umquhyle Johne Johnstoune, wrytter, and
umquhyle John Johnestoun, merchant, his sone. Ordains David, Johne, Margaret and Kathreine
Johnstoune’s lawfull bairns to the said umquhyle Johne Johnestoune, merchand, procreat
betwixe him and Jonet Wilkie, his spous, to be resavit burgesses and gildbrether of this burgh, be
rycht of the said umquhyle Johne Johnestoune, thair father, as iff the said umquhyle Johne
Johnestoune, merchand, be rycht of the said umquhyle Johne Johnestoune, his father, quha wis
burges and gildbrother of this burgh had bene admitted and ressaived burges and gildbrother of
the saniyne. Dispensing with his admissione in that caice for the quhilk this present act sal be ane
sufficient warrand to the said deyne of gild and his successors in all tyme camming.” David was
admitted B. and G. 29 Oct. 1654.

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES - 1406 - 1700.
17 March 1406-7. (P.R.)-Alisona de Duscoull facta est soror gilde tanquam heres quondam
Roberti Duscoull fratris. (Alison de Duscoull was made gild-sister as heir of umquhyle Robert
Duscoull, her brother.)
15 Nov. 1407. (P.R.)—“Dyvers persouns maid gild-brether for the dewty of x shillings].”
1 Dec. 1450. (P.R.)—“The burges air (i.e. heir) pays for his burgesschip vj.s. viij.d. He that byis
his burgesschip payis xl.s. Ane burges be richt of his wyte payis vj.s. viij.d. At this tyme many ar
maid burgessis and callit postnati et postnatae of their fatheris.”
14 June 1451. (P.R.)—Henry Rate and Mairtyne Hope, fined in xx.li. (20 [pounds]) each, for “
wrangous occupying of the fredome.”
17 May 1487.—Presens condicillus editus est per Prepositum ballivos et consuies burgi de
Edynburgh ad nomina burgensium de cetero faciendorum conservanda. Et quod unusquisque
eorundem pro libertate persolvet tres li. Excepta libertate prolium burgensium, xvijº ; die mensis
maij anno 1487. (The present list is given forth by the provost, bailies and councillors of the
burgh of Edinburgh for preserving the names of those who are henceforth to be made
burgesses. And that each one of the same shall pay three pounds for his freedom. Excepting the
freedom of the children of burgesses.—17 May 1487.)
17 May 1487.—Liber editus ad nominationem confratrum gilde huius burgi de Edinburgh per
prepositum eiusdem ballivos et consuies ad perpetuam Rei memoriam conservandam
uniusquisque predictorum fratrum pro libertate gilde predicte fabrice ecclesie quinque libras
solvendo unacum expensis clericorum et devorus debitis et consuetis conservando et reservando
pro libris burgencium sua privilegia xvij die mensis maij Anno domini millesimo
quadringentesimo octuagesimo septimo et ista sunt nomina subsequentium prepositi decani gilde
ballivorum et consuluro pro tempore. prepositus: Johanes Murray deaconus: Thomas Machin
ballivi: Wil’mus Rynd, David Craufurd, Johanes Boncle consules: Henricus Cant, Thomas Tod,
David Quhytheid, Johanes Barcase, Joh’es Twedy, Jacobus Turyng, Georgius Towris, Thomas
Shaw, Johanes Prestoun, Ricardus Hoppar, Johanes Levingston, Andreas Hervy
31 Dec. 1494—2 March 1498-9.—Andrew Bertram, provost, admitted David Mayn as burgess,
within this space of time. He is not in the lists of provosts in P.R., but appears as a bailie in 1494,
when Walter Bartraham is provost. Those admitted during these years are entered as “ Burgenses
effecti post insertain datam usque in hodiernam secundo Martii anno domini 1498.”
The next batch extends “ Ab ultima data (2 March 1498-9 usque ad f[estum] s[ancti] Michaelis
in anno i.m.v.c”. (1500).
8 Dec. 1500.—“ It was avisit and thocht expedient be Alexr. Lauder, provest, John Williamsoun,
John Adamsoun, Stevin of Borthwik, and William Todrik, bailies, and counsale for the tyme,
that the burgesses folowand suld be maid for the repairing of the town the honor and profit of the
Kirk in making of jewelry siclike as the silver candilsteks, silver crowits and uther anornaments
for the Kirk. And in likwiss that in al tymes to cum the toun be serchit of the personis indwelland
thereintill that thai may here burgesry or gild, that thai be maid and the profit thereof to be warit
upon the honor of the Kirk. Quhilk was done at the Mychelmes after the greit deid.”
The list which follows is headed “ Mercatores burgenses”—88 in all. They are indicated in the
entries by the letters “ M.B “
23 March 1507-8.—“The quhilk day It is statut & ordainit that ill tyme cuming the privilege of
burges barnis be observit and keipit in this wiss that the burges eldest son sal pay enterand as air
to his fader sal pay for his burgesry vi.s. viij.d. and for gildry entrand be his fader brother of the
gild xiij.s iiij d., and for the second son his burgesry xiij.s. iiij.d. and for his gildry xx.s. and
siclike the burgesses doichteris lauchfullie gotten to have the privilege of the secund son viz.
for the burgesry xiij.s. iiij.d. and for the gildry xx.s. Item of the unfreman entrand for his
burgesry thre li. and for his gildry five li. with the clerks fee and the utheris that accordis.”

14 March 1516-17.—Prima gildae tenta in pretorio burgi de Edynburgh coram honorabilibus
viris, David Mailvale proposito huius burgi et Wili’mo Foular decano gilde eiusdem aliis
consulibus xiiij die mensis Martii Anno M.D.C.X.V.J.to. About this time a man is entered as
being made B. by right of his father, or of his wife, whose father is frequently named, but no
further particulars are given. Every one knew every one else—the town was so small.
4 May 1518. (P.R.)—“Anent the Abbot of Narent, callit Abbot de Narentia, see in the convict
buik 26 April 1493, siclyk 4 May 1518 Ibid. quhair he is callit Robin Huid and Little Jhone.”
John White, or Quyte, was Robin Hood in the period between 31 December 1494 and 2 March
1498-9. Alexr, Carkettil was also Robin Hood.
24 May 1549. (P.R.)—“In presens of the baillies Thomas Bischop oblist him to pay to the
commoun guid the sowm of xx.li. for the profeitt of the 100 li. greitt wairing sic as mader allum
irne inbrocht in the last Flanders schip and to pay the merchant.
16 July 1550.—Quo die Johannes Makdowall effectus est fr. gilds et datur gratis de mandate
prepositi ballivorum et consulum Domino Willieimo Makdowall capellano decani gildas pro suis
devoriis (Rights or perquisites.) burgensibus et laboribus villas factis penes asdificationes
communes dicti burgi.
30 July 1550.—The Council passed an act, that no one be made freeman or burgess, except by
bailies sitting in judgement ; their names to be put in the “lokkit buke” (Now lost.) in presence of
the Dean of Guild. The duty to be paid for burgesship to be v.li. (5 pounds) and for guildry x.li.
(10 pounds), the dean to pay to the provost, bailies and clerks for the time v.li. for each of their
burgesships, and they to make no burgesses by themselves. The rights of burgesses, sons and
daughters to be observed.
10 Sept. 1550.—Quo die Johannes Ryotall lathamus gallus effectus est burgensis in judicio, et
datur eidein gratis ad requestam prioris monasterii sanctas crucis qui prepositum et ballivos in
dicto monasterio predie existen. eosdem bene tractabat.
23 Nov. 1554.—Wm. Gray, skinner, deprived of his “freedom” because he has removed himself,
his wife, and servants furth of this burgh. (C.)
8 Feb. 1554-5. (C.)—The council ordains the dean of gild to put Alexr. Bruce, gild-br., in the
“lokkit buke” (now lost).
25 Sept. 1555.—In reply to a question put by Mr. John Preston, treasurer, the provost, baillies
and counsale declare the treasurer to have no duty of burgesship yearly (i.e. the right of admitting
a burgess in virtue of his office).
26 Oct. 1555. (P.R.)—“The baillies and counsale sittand in jugment, granlis to the provest ane
fredome of ane gylry (gild-brothership) to be dystribute & gevin be him as he sail think
expedient and to quhat person he plessis.”
10 Jan. 1557-8.—Quo die nobilis vir Henricus dominus Osellus (Seigneur d’Oysel) sub
illustrissimo et christianissimo gallorum principe in his Scotias partibus locumtenens effectus est
burgensis et frater gildas ex donatione prepositi ballivoruro et consilii hujus burgi.
(The French Ambassador at the Court of the Queen Regent and Lieutenant General of the French
forces in Scotland.)
15 Feb. 1558-9.—“The baillies and counsale having consideratioun of the gude and thankful
service done be Maister John Spens the year bygane in the office of baillierie in the absence of
Edward Litill, electit baillie for this present yeir, he being in the parttis of France, ordains Johnne
Charteris dene of gyld to gyf the said Maister Jhonn Spens the dewtie (entrance fee) of ane
burgesschip and the samyn salbe allowit to him, etc.”
15 March 1560-1.—“The samyn day the baillies and counsale ordains all actis creatiouns and
privelegis of burgesses to be writtin in this buk fra this furth be writtin and extractit in our awn
maternale toung for satefeing of the commoun pepill quha hes murmurrit the Ignorance of the
style usit in this buk of before.” [But the five entries which follow, up to March, are in Latin as
of old.]
3 Feb. 1562-3. (C.)—Wm. Robertsoun, flesher, dwelling in Sanct Marye Wynd, warned under
threat of tynsale of freedom, to dwell within the town and no longer gather hides, tallow and
skins in great number and despatch the same within night to Leith, contrary to acts and statutes.
23 April 1563.—John Paterson, deacon of the masons, makes petition for free gildry, for good
service rendered on the New Tolbuith. The council answers that it is not in use to grant this
privilege to unmarried men, but when he shall happen to have a lawful wife, his desire shall be
considered and be satisfied.
27 Sept. 1563. (C.)—Jas. Abernethy deprived of his burgesship for disobedience to Thos. Cok,
town officer.
24 Dec. 1563. (C.)—“The provest, baillies and counsale ordains that na burgesship nor gildrie be
given gratis for ane yeir to cum under the pane of ten pounds to be tane of the consentar & gevar
but favour.”
7 Jan. 1563-4. (C.)—Fifty-one tavernors deprived of freedom of burgesship and gildrie, and the
keys of their houses taken away, for causing the uphald (Holding up.) of the prices and dearth
(Dearness, high price.) of wines. Seventeen were women, under their own name or as “ the
spouse of—“
8 Nov. 1564. (C.)—Duties payable for burgesship, 20 li.
„ „ for gildbrothership, 40li.
By right of apprenticeship, burgesship, 5li.
„ „ gildbrotherhood, 10 li.
14 Oct. 1566. (C.)—John Giffart has forfeit his liberty of burgesship through passing at
Whitsunday last or thereby to the town of Leith and uptaking of a house there, where he, his
household, and bairns have constantly remained.
23 Feb. 1566-7. (C.)—Wm. Byrny, B. and G., renders his freedom of B. and G. to the provost
and council, and is commanded in time coming to pay his custom, etc., and to be held as an
unfreeman, making claim to no liberty by said freedom.
9 May 1567. (C.)—(Margin— David & James Fairlie’s bairns.)—Council declairs that they will
not “ deleit the name of David Fairlie furth of the gild buke nor may not do the samyn be the law
and fynds that his bairns aucht to possess the privilege of the said act and as to James Fairlie
bairns they of right can grant them na privilege without his name be found in the buke but in
respect he was an honest man and that gif his name be not in the buke it was be negligence of
him that soucht not the samyn and in respect his fader was bayth burgess and gyld (br.) thai
promis to be gude to the said James bairns, and not to handill thame with sic extremitie as they
may of law.”
18 June 1567. (P.R.)—Act of council that no outlandish men be made burgesses till they be
married and have”stob and staik “ within the burgh, and no craftsmen save such as have
completed their apprenticeship in the said burgh.
8 Aug. 1567. (C.)—Hercules Methven, baxter, having been imprisoned for fifteen days as
accused of deforcing a town’s officer, binds himself never to do the like again, under pain of
tynsell of freedom and banishment.
25 Aug. 1567. (C.)—Hercules Methven, baxter, has his freedom restored.
15 Nov. 1567. (C.)—Charles Studeman, cook, is made G. by act of C. of 20 Nov. 1567, “and hes
satefeitt the dene of ayld for dewtie and bynds and obleisses him that fra this day furth he sail
nochtt be sene upon the calsay als the remanentt commoun kukis with meitt to sell in commoun
housses, but sail causs his servands pas with the samyn and that he sail hold his taverne on the
hie gaitt fra Witsonday furth nixtt and behaiff himseife honestlie in all tymes cumyn under the
paine of escheitt of his wynes.”
24 Dec. 1567. (C.)—The baillies and council ordains that “every man at the making of him
burges sail obleis himself to haifjak speir swerd buklar and steill bonet for serving of the baillies
and gude toun when thai haif ado & to keip the wappenshawing with the nychbors under sik
panis as may be laid to thair charge.”
6 Feb. 1567-8. (C.)—The doors of the booths of Wm. Purves, David Hoppringill, and (blank)
Craig to be closed up till they be made gildbrethren, because they sell spices which should be
sold by gildbrethren only.
27 March 1568. (P.R.).—“The dewties paid for burgesships and gild-brotherships to be applied
to bigging of kirk windokis & uther workis, through Adame Fowlertoun.”
2 April 1568. (C.)—“The caus quhy thir sowmes ar delivered to Adam Fullertoun and he to be
chargit therewith is that Alexr. Park (former) dene of gild being unable to repair the warks of the
kirk, the said Adam takes the burding thereof upoun his consent and at the counsales command
in special of thir personis quha hes lang occupeit the liberty, having na freedome, and found furth
(found out) be him.”
26 Jan. 1568-9. (C.)--The baillies and counsell “considering the great tynsell of Jhon Weir
fermorer of the pittie customs the yeir past be resson of the pest, ordains Jhone Harwood, dene of
gild, to gif to him the dewtie of ane burgesship.”
26 Sept. 1570.—“The whilk day the provest, baillies and counsall understanding the greit hurt
that cumes to the hale merchant estait of this realme be the solistatioun of lordis, greit men and
courteors quhais servands andkynsmen ar maid burgesses and fremen of burgh without paying of
any dewtie thairfor to the greit hurt of the commoun weill of all burrois And becaus sic
requeistes cannocht commounlie be refusit for eschewing of the displesour of the said greit
men and courteours. Nochtheles the said provest, baillies and counsale statutis and ordainis that
in all tymes cuming the aires of sic as ar maid burgesses or gildbroder in maner abone written
sail not bruke the fredome and libertie of burgesses bairnis nor be acceptit nor admyttit burgesses
or gild[broder] without payment of the dewtie confonne to the auld actis nochtwithstanding their
faderis fredome as said is and gyf the baillies, counsale or dene of gild consents or dois in the
contrair they to pay the said dewtie to the utmaist but favour and that this act be observit for
evir.”
25 Oct. 1570. (C.)—John Palmer, mt., is ordained to ask forgive ness of Adam Fullertoun, dean
of gild, in presence of the whole council, upon his knees, for injurious words spoken unto him,
and to deliver the keys of his booth to the baillies to remain with them till he be made gildbrother
or find caution to desist from using of gild merchandice. On 15 Nov. he is made gildbrother, and
acts himself to pay x.li. betwix and Martinmas next.
12 Sept. 1572.—Gawane Pery is made burgess gratis for good service done by him to the good
town in working at the new wester bulwark.
19 Dec. 1572.—“The quhilk day the baillies and counsall haveing respect of the gudewill borne
towartes the gude toun and nychtboures thereof be Capetane Thomas Craufurd and that he is
presentlie lyen in our Soverane Lordis service at the sege of the Castell of Edinburgh and hes to
his quarter ane gret part of the landis lyand abone the butter trone upoun the south syde of the hie
street Quhairby the said landis will be uterlie wrackit Incaiss he tak nocht gret held and cure
thairto Thairfor and for gude pleasoure to be done in tymes cuming to the gude toun Hes at his
requeist maid Mr. Robert Purwess burgess and gildbrother of this burgh frie gratis without
payment of any dewete therefor Quha gave his ayth according to the ordnance Proveiding
alwayss the said Mr. Roberts bairnis gottin or to be gottin broke (enjoy) na prevelege be vertew
of his rycht bot allanerlie himself according to the ordnance prescryvet anent the personis that
obteins their fredome and libertie gratis.
11 Feb. 1572-3.—“The samyn day the baillies and counsall haveing respect of the gude
behavioure of Walter Mackesoun and that he is not of mynde to use the tred of marchandice but
allanerlie to keep and hald ane comoun ostelar hous within this burgh Quhilk salbe ane gret
releve to the nychtboures of this burgh and that oure soverane Lordis Liegis may the mair better
be esit and servit within the samyn thrby Hes admittet the said Walter to be their buigess and
gildbrother for payment of the dewete of twentie pound allanerlie Notwithstanding of the act
maid in the contrair that nane sould be ressavit but payment of three scoir pound Qlk act the said
baillies & counsall be thir presents dispensis with for and in respect of the premises.”
13 Feb. 1572-3.—“The quhilk day the baillies and counsall being convenit comperit Johne Neill
skynnar sone and apperand air of Rychart Neill skynnar burgess of this brugh and presentet his
said fatheris ticket of burgesship and in respect thereof desyred to be admittet their burgess be
vertew of his said fatheris prevelege for payment of the Dewete usit and wonat Qlk prevelege the
saids baillies and counsall wald not consent that he should broke In respect that the said
Ry[char]t wes within this brugh the tyme of the Detention thereof agains our Soverane Lord and
that there wes ane ordinance maid that sik persones that remanet within the samyn suld tyne thair

1 Oct. 1574.—“ Robert Abercromby, saidler, being dischairgit of his fredome of burgesshipe
and gildrye for making bargane with ane unfreman in Leyth and culloring (colouring) of his

9 Nov. 1576. (C.)—“The provest, baillies & counsall ordains that all sic as hes bene burgesses

10 July 1577. (C.)—“The bailyeis and counsall ordains the unfree bonnet makkers to be

1 Jan. 1577-8.—“The provest, baillies and counsale remembering the monyfald benifitts resavet
be them for their commounweill be the moyane of Robert Campbell, ane of the scribis of our
souerane lordis sessioun, and houpping the samyn gude will to continew with him, Thay grants
gavis and disponis to him and his airis lawfull gottin or to be gottin the fredome of ane privelege
of fre-burgesses and gyld-broder and they did resave his aith according to their consuetude in
sick caiss.”
8 Oct. 1578.—“The provest, bailleis and counsell understanding that Lucas Willsoun, dene of
gild, hes oversein himself in making of Thomas Bell burges and gildbrother for the soume of
threttie punds allanerlie, it being statuit that nane sail pass the said dignitie under the soum of
fourtie pund at lest Quhairfoir thay ordane the said Thomas Bell to deliver to the said dene of
gild ten pund in compleit payment of fourtie pund and that nane heirefter be maid burges nor
gildbrother except thay be admittit in presens of the provest, bailleis and counsell or at the lest
the maist part thereof.”

3 Nov. 1591.—A new form of oath was ordained in respect so many burgesses take little or no
regard to the keeping of their burgess oath, especially in regard to extents, watching, etc. This
oath ran as follows (7 Dec. 1591):—

                             THE AlTHE OF ANE GILDBROTHER.
“ I sail give the best counsall I can and conceil the counsall schawin to me. I sail not consent to
dispone the comoun gude but for ane comoun caus and ane comoun proffate. I sail mak concorde
quhair discorde is to the uttermost of my powars. I sail give leal and trw jugement on all
occatiouns and nychtbourheidis but pryce prayer or reward. Swa help me God.”
The prayer of invocation used at the meeting of the Guild Council:—“0 most gratious God and
loveing father we most humblle beseik thy majestie for thy Chryst’s saik to be present in meting
with us, in giveing ane blissing to owr affaires and seing thow art only wyse be thow owr
wisdome in all owr adoes And grant (all partialitie and all corrupt affections set assyd) we may
deall in all maters presentit to us with upryght hearts and single eyes as in thy presence, sua that
the issuit of our travells by thy speciall grace may alwayes tend to the glorie of thy name the
weillfair of this our native toun and the comfort of everie faithfull member of the same through
Jesus Christ our Lord and only Saviour. Sobeit. Amen.”
15 Apr. 1600.—Mr. Wm. Watson, born 1558. Minister in St. Giles. Put in ward Jan. 1586 for
speaking boldly before the King. An intimate friend of James Melville, who gave him shelter at
Kilrennie when order was given for his apprehension as being concerned in the tumult of 17 Dec.
1596. He was released from the horn and restored in July 1597, but owing to his refusal to accept
the King’s story of the Gowrie conspiracy, he was banished for a time in 1600. He was one of
the eight ministers summoned in 1606 to appear before the King at Greenwich, and was warded
with Dr. Vaughan, Bishop of London. In 1607 he returned to his parish of Burntisland, whence
he was translated in 1615 to Markinch, where he died in 1619.
In 1617 James VI. paid his first and only visit to Scotland after his succession to the English
crown. The nobles, gentlemen and household who attended the banquet given on the 26th June
were made burgesses and gildbrethren gratis.

7 March 1660.—Sir James Stanfield of New Milns, in East Lothian, and his son Philip. Sir
James, a Yorkshire man by birth, is said to have been a colonel on the Parliamentary side in the
Civil War. He came to Scotland, after the battle of Dunbar, 1650, and having acquired certain
lands on the south bank of the Tyne, a mile east of Haddington, he set up a cloth manufactory,
named New Milns. Later he was knighted by Charles II., and his cloth industry was encouraged
in 1681 by Tames, Duke of Albany and York, later James VII.
He also acquired property in Edinburgh, both in Blackfriars Wynd, and in what is now called
World’s End Close, where Sir Wm. Bruce of Ba’lcaskie disponed part of his property to him,
whence the close at one time bore the name of Stanfield’s Cl. He also owned the ground in Leith
whereon the glass work was built later. He was made a burgess and guild-brother of Edinburgh
7th March 1660, being then secretary to General Major Thomas Morgan, gratis, and 5 pounds
voted to him, for his good service done to the town.
On 2 July 1679 Mr. Philip Stanfield, fiar of New Milne, was made burgess and guild-brother of
the burgh, gratis. He must have been Sir James’ elder and most unsatisfactory son, who was
married, and lived in his father’s house. On the 28 November the body of Sir James was found
among the ice in a pool in the river. It was secretly buried by his son, as that of a suicide.
But the Lord Advocate, hearing of the case, gave orders for the exhumation and examination of
the corpse. This was carried out, and the surgeons performed the autopsy, in the course of which
they made an incision in the neck of the deceased.
When Philip, at the request of the surgeons, lifted the head of his dead father, to help in replacing
the body in the coffin, the blood suddenly showed on the linen swathing, and Philip, horror-
struck, dropped his burden, and fell back in a faint. In due course he was arrested, and tried
before the High Cour t of Justiciary in February 1688, and found guilty. Sir George Mackenzie
assisting the Lord Advocate in the prosecution. He was hanged at the Market Cross, and his body
was hanged in chains at the Gallow Lee, between Edinburgh and Leith, and finally disappeared.
The New Milns property was sold, on the winding up of the cloth company, to the notorious
Colonel Francis Charteris, who changed its name to Amisfield, after that of his family seat in
Nithsdale. (See “Twelve Scots Trials,” by Wm. Roughead, W.S., and “ Sir Richard” in Sir
Walter Scott’s “ Minstrelsy of the Scottish Borders.”)

In the early admissions of burgesses payments of duty were sometimes “by composition.” In
some cases spices and wine, a banquet in fact, were furnished, and accepted. Burgesses were
often admitted by the provost, or a bailie, or the treasurer, apart from the Dean of Guild Court.
When thus admitted by a bailie, it was by him as a bailie “ et ea ratione.” This was corrected
later. A master often is admitted burgess in order to be able to take an apprentice. The date,
between brackets, in the entry of admission of a craftsman as B. or G. by right of his
apprenticehip, is that of his entering his master’s service. When a letter is given in brackets in a
name, as in “Caldwell(s),” it indicates that both forms (“ Caldwell “ and “ Caldwells “) are
found.
A good many entries appear twice, under different dates. If “gratis” be not mentioned, the
burgess paid for his burgesship.
Dates.—It must be remembered that under the Old Style the year ended 24 March. Thus 1 Jan.
1500 (o.s.) succeeds 31 Dec. 1500, and should be written 1 Jan. 1500-1. The New Style was
adopted 1st Jan. 1600.
There are very few addresses or residences given, e.g. “ John Adamsone fornent the crose.” 12
Jan. 1570-1
John Hamilton, “ dwelland in Williamson’s Close,” 14 Jan. 1567-8.
Residence.—When a man was made a burgess of Edinburgh it was necessary for him to reside
within the burgh. Instances occur frequently of indwellers in Leith, who, on being made
burgesses, are required to remove and find residence in Edinburgh, under the paine of tinsell
(loss) of their freedome, eg. Francis Aird and Rob. Dowglas, 27 Oct. 1669. Patrick Crightoun,
mt. was forced to leave the Canongate and reside in Edinburgh 17 March 1648.
An applicant for burgesship could choose one qualification therefor, rather than another—
probably preferring the cheaper. Thus a man eligible as ‘prenteis to an employer, or as guidson to
a burgess, would choose the latter qualification.
Not infrequently a group of one trade entered as burgesses at one time—a bunch of tailors,
hatmakers. or fleshers, while on special occasions, such as banquets, or the honouring of a
special family, as many as a hundred might be admitted burgesses and gild-brethren, gratis. Such
burgesses, however, as a rule, enjoyed the privilege personally, without the right to transmit it to
their bairns.
Moses Mosias, a Jew, was allowed to trade in the town, with a promise, for his encouragement,
that if he become a Christian, he shall be admitted burgess, gratis (M.T.C. 14 Dec. 1698.)
           NOTES ON BURGESS ROLL, 1701-1760.
The dates quoted in the Burgess Roll of the admission of a burgess or guild
brother by the Town Council are frequently incorrect, and sometimes cannot be
traced. A number of those admitted by the Council were never admitted by the
Dean of Guild and his court ; their names are not on the register, and consequently
do not appear in the MS. Index. Occasionally a
burgess is admitted by the Guild Court by an act of Council passed some time
after! Nor was admission by the Town Council promptly followed by that of the
Guild Council—we find, for instance, Wm. Lumsdain was admitted by the Town
Council 5 Sept. 1744—and only six years later, 12 Oct. 1750, did the Guild
Council admit him. John Russel, writer to the signet, admitted by the Town
Council 5 Aug. 1741, became B. and G. only on 15 Sept. 1749, after eight years’
delay, while Dr. Robert Hay waited for nearly ten years, from 28 May 1740 to 10
Jan. 1750, ere he became a “freeman.”

But the apprentices were far more dilatory.
 Robert Thomson, skinner, entered p. 18 July 1711, burgess 18 Feb. 1747.
 John Somervail, wright, entered p. 3 Mar. 1797, burgess 11 Feb. 1736.
 Robert Young, wright, entered p. 25 Oct. 1682, burgess 19 Sept. 1722.
 Robert Tod, wright, entered p. 18 July and 22 Aug. 1705; burgess 7 Mar. 1750.

Evidently there was no advantage to be gained by early admission.
The same may be noticed in the case of guild brethren, entering sometimes long
after admission as burgesses.

It is quite evident that despite all the care taken in entering apprentices, burgesses
and guild brethren, omissions have occurred. We find men admitted burgesses as
apprentices who are not entered in the apprentice roll ; or others entered by right
of a father burgess, whom we seek in vain in the burgess roll.

Occasionally the Council passed a second act admitting some one as B. and G.,
apparently forgetting that this had been done already.

Admission as a burgess and guild brother without payment of dues—
“gratis”—was in many cases purely complimentary, and conferred no rights or
privileges, unless particularly specified.

In some cases it was granted “for good service done,” such as the admission of
Wm. Blair, gratis, “for good service done at the late fire in the head of the West
Bow (29 Sept. 1710)

In at least one case the widow of a burgess and guild brother seems to have
conferred the right of admission on her serond husband. See Thomas Espline, 30
Aug. 1710.

Note.—The form of the entry in the Minutes of Town Council differs occasionally
so far from that in the Burgess Roll as to make it worth while to note both. Where
no “right of admission “ is mentioned, the admission is by payment as exigible
from an “unfreeman.”

The paucity of cutlers within the city may be gauged by the entry of Robert Boog,
26 Apr. 1748, when there was “no quorum of their craft within the city,” and the
Town Council had to assume the responsibility. Chairmasters seem to have been
admitted invariably on payment of the dues as unfreemen. They served no
apprenticeship, and, curiously enough, seem to have had no right by parentage or
marriage.
19 Mar. 1701.—Act discharging unfree traders to keep shops, cellars, etc. for
selling wares, drink; also prohibiting burgesses.to keep more shops or cellars than
one, contrary to law ; offenders’ shops to be shut and themselves amerciat at the
discretion of Dean of Gild and Council.

11 Apr. 1701.—“The same day the Council taking to their serious consideration
the great prejudice the old burgesses and their children and these that have served
their ‘prenticeship or have bought their freedome in this cittie doe daylie sustaine
by gratis burgesses who oft times doe make moyen with one or other of the
Council to get a gratis burges ticket upon designe either to get a place or to get
their children put in Heriott’s Hospitall or themselves into the Trinity Hospitall or
both—which does much prejudice, etc.” No gratis burgess ticket shall henceforth
entitle to these privileges.

21 May 1701.—All gratis burgesses must compear before the Dean of Gild and
his Council and take the oaths before extracting of the burges ticketts.

27 June 1701.—Act of Council in favour of the freemen burgesses. The following
acts were exhibited, and appointed to be intimate yearly by tuck of drum, against
abuses committed by unfree persons in the land mercat and elsewhere, viz. :
  Act of 8 May 1607 ;
  16 July 1647 ;
  17 Oct. 1656 ;
  14 Feb. 1688,

forbidding hawking at private houses except on the market day, viz. Wednesday,
between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m., between the Weigh-house and the Luckenbooths. None
allowed to sit down in front of the stands but must take stands for themselves. No
retailers (hucksters) allowed, only makers of what they sell. No one allowed to
keep unsold goods within the town. The bailie of the Butter Mercat empowered to
put this into effect.

25 Feb. 1702.—John Kerbie admitted burgess—“hattmaker; full rights granted on
payment of dues of apprentice in respect of his singular airt in making of hatts and
weaving,” by act of C.

M.T.C., 18 Mar. 1702.—“ The same day the Council prohibits and discharges the
Incorporation of the Baikers and other Incorporations of this city in all tyme
coming to cotnmunicat the freedome of the trade to any in the head of the
Cannogate or any other place within this burgh but to such who are burgesses, and
appoynts the several corporations to cause record thir
presents in their respective books and return ane extract of the same to the
Councill.”

30 June 1702.—“The same day the Lord Dean of Gild and his Council in
obedience to the Act of the Lords of her Maj. Privie Councill anent the takeing the
oath of alleadgeance and subscryveing the same with the assurance to her Maj.,
did accordingly take and subscryve the same.”

26 June 1702.—“Anthony Leureux, french hatter, gives in a petition shewing that
he, being admitted ane freeman in the Incorporation of the Hattmakers, upon a
gratis burgess tickett, from the Councill, upon the account of his singular art in
making of hatts : and having as a freeman applyed to the Dean of Gild and his
Councill for booking ane apprentice, they refused the same, in respect of his gratis
burgess tickett, and therefor craving the Councill to ordaine his apprentice to be
received and booked seeing he payed ane valuable consideration to the
Incorporation of the Hattmakers. Which being
considered be the Councill, they appoynt the Dean of Gild and his Councill to
admit and receave the petitioner to be burgess of this burgh for payment of the
dues of ane apprentice in respect he served his apprenticeship to ane hattmaker,
and his master neglected to book him.” (The ‘prentice in question was David, s. to
John Leurie, cupper in France, who entered as ‘prentice the same day, 15 July.)
(15 July 1702.)

29 July 1752.—Benjamin Ramage, p. to Adam Watkins, H.M. Printer and
Stationer for Scotland, B. In the privately printed “Reminiscences” (p. xxxv) of
Charles Cowan of Logan House, ex-M.P., speaking of the paper mills at
Valleyfield, Penicuick, he says, “’they were occasionally possessed and wrought
by the King’s printer of the day. There is a tradition in the parish that a King’s
printer, named Watkins, about the middle of last (i.e. 18th) century met with a very
appalling death. He had been a very godless man, and one Sunday he had been
walking with a friend towards Pennicuick House during
the hours of divine service, when a storm of thunder and lightning suddenly set in ;
he blasphemously defied the power of the Almighty, and was immediately struck
down dead. It created a great sensation in the congregation, who were informed of
the death by the officiating minister before the close of the service.”

21 Nov. 1711.—The Dean of Guild represented to the Council that in obedience to
their appointment, 7 Feb. last, he caused call for Thomas Vint and James
M’Culloch their burgess tickets, and also caused close up their chop doors and
mark the recalling of their admissions in the Dean of Gild Books. But since the
said Thomas Vint has at his own hand without any licence either of the Council or
Dean of Gild Court opened his chop and exercised his employment as formerly,
upon which the said Dean of Gild caused close up his chop of new again. Upon
which the said Thomas Vint has raised summonds of reduction and improbation
and by vertue thereof caused sumond the said Dean of Gild to compear before the
Lord of Council and Session, and therefore the Dean of Guild desired the Council
might stand by and defend him in what he had done, in the said matter by their
appointment. The Council approved of the Dean of Gild’s procedure, and
appointed their lawyers and agent to be employed to defend him upon the Town’s
expenses.

28 Apr. 1712.—The Merchant Company complain of evils arising from false and
improper designations given to persons admitted as burgesses and guild brethern.
The Council ordain that no one be admitted until his claim be openly read and
approved by Dean of Guild and his Council, and that his particular business be
designed in his burges ticket, and a full record kept.

25 June 1712.—(George Bailie.)-—The Maiden Hospital was in 1695 founded by
the craftsmen of Edinburgh and Mary Erskine, relict of James Hair, druggist,
burgess of Edinburgh, she being “ the first who projected and destinated funds for
Maiden Hospitals in the City of Edinburgh.” She accordingly bears the Title of the
Founder of the Hospital, and it is provided that two of the name of Erskine shall be
for ever governours thereof, named in the first instance by herself—these two
being (probably as relatives) the notorious Master James Erskin of Grange,
Senator of the College of Justice, who marooned his mad wife in St. Kilda, and
Master David Erskine, advocate. The governors, by grant from the Town Council,
enjoyed the right of nominating one man annually for admission as a burgess
gratis.

7 Sept. 1716.—“The Council upon report of Robert Craig, Dean of Gild, and
considering that the eight tickets given to the magistrates yearly being derogative
to the credit of the good toun, and prejudiciall to the Dean of Gild and his Court,
for preventing whereof it is statut and ordained that from and after Mertemas next
the Dean of Gild for the tyme being pay to the Lord Provost two hundred pound
yearly and to each of the other Magistrates one hundred pounds Scots yearly in
lew of their tickets. And siclyke statut and ordained that from and after the said
terme the Council dispose of burges and gild brother tickets at the rate following,
viz. : each burges and gild brother ticket not under two hundred me’rks and each
singall burges ticket not under one hundred merks Scots money.”

26 Oct. 1716.—Table of dues for the weigh-houses of Edinburgh and Leith.
Unfreemen pay twice what burgesses pay.

22 Mar. 1717.—Act of Council, in view of abuses in persons, other than
burgesses, keeping shops, etc., that in future any one wishing to be made a
burgess, and having right thereto, must enter within three years after their
minority, or marriage, or expiry of apprenticeship, otherwise they shall lose the
right, and also pay twenty pounds Scots for each year they shall so trade. Farther
that no women, other than widows or daughters of burgesses, shall be allowed to
keep, shops, and this in special view of the fact that so many servants quit service
and open shops, causing dearth of servants and unfair competition.
And farther, that no one be eligible for any office, which necessitates guild
brotherhood, unless he be already a guild brother.

12 June 1717.—Mr. Wm. Aikman of Cairnie made B. and G., gratis, for painting
three framed pictures (duly paid for !) of King George, King William, and Queen
Mary.

toun’s friends as his Lordship shall think fitt. And recommends to Bailie Hope to
writt to his Lordship to keep an list of the persons names and designations in order
to be recorded.”

16 Oct. 1717.—“Grissell Pillans is impowered to trade within the citty as ane

16 July 1718.—In consequence of a petition given in by the maltmen and brewers
of Leith against unfreemen who have taken up the trade of brewing in Leith,
underselling the legitimate brewers, and encouraging smuggling and hidden trade,
the Town Council discharge all persons other than burgesses of Edinburgh and
incorporate maltsters of Leith to take up or carry on the trade of brewing in Leith,
under pain of one hundred merks Scots. A number of unfree brewers in Leith
entered burgesses of Edinburgh accordingly.
10 Sept. 1718.—£200 Scots paid to Treasurer of the Merchant Maidens Hospital,
and £100 Scots to the deacon convener of Trades, in lieu of compliment of
disposal of two and one burgess tickets respectively, as was the custom formerly.

them lately in lieu of these tickets, upon condition that they have worn velvet coats

sterling shall be paid to the Treasurers
of the Merchants and Trades Maiden Hospitals in equal portions, power being

22 July 1719.—“Edinburgh, the twenty-second day of Jully one thousand seven
hundred and nynteen years. The which day the Councill appointed the Dean of
Gild and his Councill to admitt and receave John Law, Lord and Earle of

Kingdom of France, to be burgess and gild brother be right of John Law of
Lauriston, burgess and gild brother, his father. Dispensing with the dues.”

22 July 1719.—John Law, Lord and Earl of Tankerville. This is not the
Tankerville family of Bennet, at Chillingham, but its namesake in France on the
river Seine. In “ Les Ecossais en France” (Francisque-Michel), 1862, Vol. II, p.
423, speaking of this famous John Law, the author states that the Laws of
Lauriston are not the direct descendants of the financier. “Cette famille est issue
du frere de 1’inventeur du systeme, qui 1’avait rejoint en France et fut compris
avec lui. La Duchesse de Bourbon fit placer les deux neveux de John Law au
service dans les Indes orientales. L’ain£, Jacques Francois Law, comte de
Tancarville devint chevalier de Saint Louis, etc.” He adds a note on “Tancarville”
:— “ Cette terre venait, a ce quil parait, de John Law. Dangeau ecrit dans son
Journal, a la date du 31 aout 1718. ‘ On dit que le comte d’Evreux a vendu la
terre de Tancarville a M. Law, qui lui en donne 650,000 livres et une pension
viagere de 6000 francs.’ “
In the letterpress of Turner’s “ Rivers of France “ (published by J. M’Cormick,
147 Strand, London, N.D. Letterpress in both French and English), the note on the
front view of the Castle states that “a portion of the building is comparatively new
having been built by the celebrated projector, Law, who, immediately after he had
bought the property for eight hundred thousand francs, was obliged to fly the
kingdom.” He died in obscurity and poverty in Venice, his grave is in the church
of San Moise.

22 July 1719.—Sir Archibald Primrose of Dunipace
In 1661 Sir John Foulis of Ravelston md. Margaret, dr. of Sir Archd. Primrose of
Dunipace, half-sister of Archd., 1st Earl of Roseberry. Their son and heir, George,
assumed the name of Primrose on succeeding to the estate of Dunipace, but was
evidently known popularly by his patronymic, Foulis, as in this entry.
The Sir Archibald, now made B. and G., was executed at Carlisle, 5 Nov. 1746,
for his adherence to the Stewart family in the rising of the ‘45.

   “ praeclari sui de viri virtuti Judicii testes Civium Suorum numero
   “ Adscriptum voluerunt” ;
which is for holding the burges ticket given to the Right Honourable John Law,

23 Aug. 1721.—“James Bayne, musicall instrument maker, presented the Councel

and motto on the head thereof. Which they accepted of and delyvered to the Lord
Provost, and appointed the same to be transmitted by his Lordship to his
successors. And the Councel considering it is the interest of every societie and
community to incouradge men of ingenuity and spirit, therefore they appointed the
Dean of Gild and his Councel to admitt and receave the said James Bayne to be
burges and gild brother of this citie and declaired his admission to be als valid and
effectuall to him as if he had payed be an unfreeman. Dispensing with the dues.”
(Margin, “This act rescinded as per act the 15 Janry. 1724. And the Lord Provost
allowed to dispose of the within milln to such as his Lordship shall think fitt”)
