17 Oct. 1722.—Act in favour of Charles Dallas, for delivery of his burges ticket,
of which he had been deprived, and also fined, for printing and publishing a paper
called the Edinburgh News Letter, containing several scandalous speeches and
poems, without licence, contrary to an act of Council. He pleads ignorance of the
said act, blushes for and is ashamed of his action, and has found caution to behave
himself civilly and forbear the like practices in time coming.

25 Mar. 1724.—James Brownhill, wright, late burgess and guild brother, had been
convicted of being accessory to an attempt made on the house of Andrew
Wardrope, late Deacon convener, for the purpose of seizing a banner or ensign
belonging to the craftsmen of the city. Part of his punishment was the loss of his
freedom as burgess and guild brother. He is now most penitent and craves
reinstatement, which is granted. (Builder of “James” Court, Lawnmarket.)

10 Apr. 1724.—Four blank burgess and guild brother tickets to be signed by the
town clerk and sent to the Lord Provost, now in London, to be filled up by him as
he shall think fit.

15 Apr. 1724.—The same day Bailie Archibald Wallace reported that John Corse,
writer in Edinburgh, having excerpted from the records of this kingdom under his
care, as keeper appointed by the Lord Register, an exact note of several charters
under the Great Seal in favours of the town of Edinburgh since the year 1366 and
of several donations and letters of gift and confirmation under the Privy Seal since
the year 1500, as also several unprinted Acts of Parliament and Ratifications
particular and general made in favours of the good town of Edinburgh and
community thereof since the year 1483 to the year 1707, and that the said John had
delivered the same to him for the good town’s use, which being considered by the
Council, they with the extraordinary Deacons, appointed the said list to be put in
the charter house, there to be kept for the good town’s use; and for these and other
good services appointed the Dean of Guild and his Council to admit and receive
the said John Corse, burgess and guild brother ; dispensing with the dues,
declaring his admission to be as valid and effectual as
if he had paid the whole dues in use to be paid by an unfreeman.

25 Sept. 1724.—The College Treasurer reported that the deceased David Chrystie,
periwig-maker, burgess, had by disposition of 10 Mar. 1724 disponed to the
Magistrates, Ministers, and Town Council, for the maintenance of the name of
Chrystie, and specially of him that shall be a student of philosophy or divinity in
the College, the high dwelling on the east side of the head of Liberton’s Wynd.
(His brother.g;erman James was made B. and G. the same day in respect of the
said disposition.)

11 Nov. 1724.—City Treasurer appointed to pay to James Mitchelson, late Deacon
of the Goldsmiths and convener of the crafts, £ 10 stg. in lieu of a burgess ticket
(to be disposed of by him) for his good service to the Council the year of his
office, as has been in use to be paid to his predecessors, conveners of the craft.

2 Dec. 1724.—Margaret Blair, shopkeeper, is allowed by the court to trade during
life or her being unmarried, for payment of fifty merks Scots money to be allowed
in part payment of her husband’s dues in case she happens to marry.

23 Dec. 1724.—Ann Strachan, merchant, compearing, is hereby authorised to
trade and merchandise in this faurgh dureing her lifetime because she has payd on
that account one hundred merks and declairs that in case she shall happen to be
married to an unfreeman that the foresaid sum shall be allowed in part of his entry
money.
9 July 1725.—“Committee appointed to bring in the draught of an act for
preventing of the making of burgesses who are not able to bear the character, and
soon after become burdensome on the citie.”

1 Sept. 1725.—Act discharging any burgess and guild brother ticket to be
delivered to any person admitted, until first they pay the dues to the Dean of
Guild.

1 Sept. 1725 (entered after 22 Sept.)—The Lord Provost, Bailies, Council, and
Deacons of Crafts, considering the arrears due to the Dean of Guild’s accepting
bills and other securities in payment of dues of burgess and gild brother’s tickets,
whereby receivers of such tickets and their children enjoy the benefits and
privileges of the city without having paid therefor, ordain that no one paying for
his burgess ticket by bill or other security, shall receive said ticket till the Dean of
Gild be satisfied and the dues paid, and no clerk shall extend or give out any such
ticket without the Dean of Guild’s warrant.

3 May 1727.—The Council upon a petition given in be William Atkine, merchant
burgess of Edinburgh, and upon information from the Magistrates, the Council
recommended to them to call for the petitioners burgess ticket and take it from him
and to discharge him to exercise the privileges of a burgess within this city in time
coming.

20 Nov. 1728.—“The same day the Court having upon inquiry found that John
Tirie, stabler, who was booked burges upon the sexth instant as son to John Tirie,
ribbon-weaver, hath imposed on the court by bringing persons to attest him to be
the son of the said John Tirie which he hath this day acknowledged to be false, doe
therefor appoint his admission to be expung’d and his ticket to be lacerat, which
was accordingly done in face of court, and he discharged to trade as ane
unfreeman.”

9 Apr. 1729.—Committee appointed to prepare an act empowering the Dean of
Guild and his successors and court to grant licenses to those who have a small
trade and are not able to enter burgesses.
23 Apr. 1729.—Dean of Guild and his court empowered to grant liberty to
inhabitants of both sexes, unable to purchase their “freedom,” to deal and trade in
retail of ale, beer, fish, herbs, roots, fruits, cowfeeding, horsehiring, poultry and
the like, to be renewed annually, dues not to exceed ten pounds or be under three
pound, and proper record kept.

9 July 1727.—“The Councel with the extraordinar deacons approved of the
following recept:—Edinburgh, day of years. In consideration that B. has paid to A.
Dean of Guild for the use of this city the sum of , is heirby permitted by the sd.
Dean of Gild and his Councel to exercise traide within this city and its libertys by
allenerly for a term of one year from to exclussive without any furder right or
priviledge to the sd. .” Extracted by

22 Oct. 1729.—Act of Council ordaining that in future, in the interests of
economy, no entertainments at the expense of the city shall be given on the
occasion of the making of noblemen and others burgesses and guild brethren, and
any member of Council proposing a name for such honour shall pay for the
burgess ticket, except in the case of His Majesty’s ministers of state and certain
others.

26 Nov. 1729.—“Euphane Gutrie, relict of Patrick Hirdman, is hereby allowed to
trade dureing her vidouity in this city haveing payed to the Dean of Gild five
pound for her said lycence.”

5 Aug. 1730.—“The same day the Council appointed the Dean of Gild and his
Council to admitt and receave the persons after named, viz. : Nicholas
Dassauville, carpenter; Charles Proy, reedmaker ; Thomas Carlier; James Charlet;
John Dassauville ; Francis Brochart; Claud Polain ; John Dallet, all weavers of
Cambrick of the County of Picardy in France, all to be burgesses of this citie for
encouragement of the traide of cambrick makeing.” [It was from these natives of
Picardie that the district at the east end of York Place, took, and keeps, its name of
Picardy.]

25 Sept. 1730.—“The Council with the Extraordinar Deacons considering it is the
interest of the common wealth that William Muir, alias Moor, prisoner within the
Tolbooth of this citie, should be prosecuted for the crimes wherewith he stands
charged, do appoint a prosecution to be carried on agst. him for the sd. crymes
before the Lord Provost as high Shirriff within this citie or his Deput accordingly.
And the thesaurer or his successor in office to depurse what expence shall be
thereto necessary.”

2 June 1731.—The Council considering the act of Council of 24 Dec. 1703
limiting the import of gratis burgess tickets to a term of five years, and considering
that there is no distinction made in the tenor of gratis tickets that are given to such
as are servants to H.M. Commissioners to the General Assembly, and to such like,
from the honorary tickets that are given to noblemen and gentlemen in
compliment, do ordain that hereafter in all gratis tickets which are not given in
compliments to noblemen and gentlemen, that there shall be an explicit reference
to the said act of Council, limiting the term for which the freedom is thereby
intended, and appoints the gratis tickets granted 26 May to the Earl of Loudon’s
servants to be made out after that tenor.

30 June 1731.—Formula of gratis burgess ticket:—“ Edinburgh, the day of . The
which day in presence of the right honourable Patrick Lindesay, Esq., Lord
Provost of this city, Thomas Dick, Alexander Wilson, Robert Blackwood and
James Seton, Bailies, John Osborn, Dean of Gild and Gild Council, compearing,
A. B. is made Burgess of this Burgh in termes of and conform to ane Act of the
Town Council dated the thirty day of June 1731. Extra(cte)d. P. Lindesay,
Provost.”

8 Mar. 1732.—“Considering that by the minutes the second of February last the
Dean of Gild and his Council are only appointed to admit and receive Principal
Osburn and Professor Chalmers burgesses and gild brethren in ample form,
whereas it was the intention of the Council that they should be made burgesses and
gild brethren in the best manner, dispensing with payment of any dues, for good
services done by them to the town, appointed the Dean of Gild and his Council to
admit and receive them accordingly.”
6 Apr. 1732.—Liberty granted to Patrick Hog, sometime tenant in Beanston, and
(blank) Craig, his wife, and the survivor of them to occupy and follow any trade or
business within this city or its liberties as fully as any burgess or gild brother can
lawfully do, during the Council’s pleasure. Dispensing with payment of any dues
in consideration of good services done to the city.

12 Apr. 1732.—Upon considering a petition from Charles Milne, writer to the
signet, craving damages done to some houses in Potterrow during the late
unnatural Rebellion, in fortifying the town, appointed the Dean of Gild and
Council to admit and receive him to be burgess and gild brother be right of Robert
Milne of Balfarge, mason, his deceased father, dispensing with
payment of dues to the town, and appointed precept of clare constat to be made in
favour of Susanna Weir, his spouse, for infefting of her as heir to Walter Weir, her
uncle, in the said houses in Potterrow, which hold feu of the town, dispensing with
payment of any composition or bygone feu-duty, in full satisfaction of any claim
which he may have for any such damages.

3 May 1732.—“The same day the Dean of Gild and his Council grant liberty and
licence to Patrick Hogg, tennent in Beanstoun, and (blank) Craig, his spouse, and
to the longest liver of them, to occupy and follow trade within this city or libertys
as any burges or gild brother can lawfully doe, dispensing with the payment of
dues for good services done to the good town, conform to ane act of Town
Councill of the date the twenty-sexth day of Aprile last.”

14 Feb. 1733.—Licence to Henry van Winegarden, distiller, to trade in this city

23 Oct. 1734.— Brigadier Moyle to be entertained at his admission as burgess and
guild brother of this city.

5 Feb. 1735.—“An honorary burgess ticket to Alexr. Montgomerie, dated 2 Aug.
last, was produced by Dean of Gild Simpson, and upon a motion made by him,
was cancelled, in respect that there was a misnomination of the person. The person
intended by the Marquis of Lothian, late Commissioner to the General Assembly,
to have had the foresaid ticket being James Scot, tayler in Edinburgh, and
therefore the Dean of Gild and his Council were appointed to admit and receive
the said James Scot to be a honorary burgess of this city in common form.”

29 Aug. 1735.—Paid one pound ten shillings stg. for the three trumpeters
attending the Duke of Buccleugh being made burgess.

19 Nov. 1735. —The Council considering that as there are several processes now
in dependance before the Court of Session whereto the city is a party which may
occasion an appeal to the House of Lords, whence it is expedient that councillors
at London, learned in law, ought to be timeously retained by the city. Did
therefore resolve that” William Murray, Esq., be accordingly retained, and that
Provost Lindsay do the same.

2 Feb. 1737.—Owing to the great number of applications for relief from persons
only recently admitted as burgesses, the Council resolve that no demands of this
nature shall be remitted to the committee of younger date than seven years.
(Minutes of Town Council.) 8 June 1737,—The Hon. Sir John Barnard, one of the
members of Parliament for the city of London, B. and G., gratis, for good services.
A silver box to be made for the burgess ticket, and to be transmitted to Sir John in
London.

19 July 1738.—Committe appointed to revise and examine the rates of upsetts and
entries of burgesses and gild brethren and report how much the same ought to be
increased.

1 Feb. 1740.—“ Considering that the Rt. Honble. James, Earle of Murray, has
made a present of forty pounds sterling to be distributed towards relief of the poor
of this city and Canongate, which Treasurer Shairp has received and wherewith he
is to debit himself, therefore (the Council) did appoint the Dean of Gild and his
Council to admit and receive the said Earl of Murray and the Honble. Francis and
Henry Stewarts, his bretheren german, to be burgesses and gild bretheren of this
city in most ample form.”

6 Feb. 1740.—“Reported by the Lord Provost that the Earl of Hopeton and his son
Lord Hope have made a present of one hundred pounds sterling to be distributed to
the poor of this city as the Magistrates thought proper for their relief in this
rigorous season, and that his Lordship had returned the said noble Earl and his son
a letter of thanks.” (Both made honorary burgesses and gild brethren.)

6 Feb. 1740.—Charles Hope Weir of Craigiehall. Of the great Hope family,
second son of the ist Earl of Hopetoun, married 26 July 1733 Catharine, only dr.
and heir of Sir Wm. Weir of Blackwood, Lanarkshire. Their eldest son, William,
took the name of Hope-Vere.

8 Sept. 1742.—Eleanor Aitkinson, spouse to Daniel Forbes, writer, is licentiat to
trade within this city dureing her life, she having paid to the Dean of Gild one
hundred merks Scots money for her said liberty.” (Margin, “ Mrs. Forbes, £1 : 11:
1.4.”).

8 Feb. 1744.—Thomas Kid, late mt. in Dundee, now residing in Leith, B. and G.,
be r. of his dec. w. Rachael, dr. to dec. Mr. Wm. Eccles, doctor of physic, B. and
G., although the Dean of Gild had “demurred to make the petitioner burges and
gild brother in right of his wife because she dyed some few months before the
petitioner’s application without authority from the Town Council.” Precedent
quoted of Mr. Walter Heart, 1 Feb. 1723. This priviledge not to be granted to any
one hereafter.

8 Feb. 1744.—“The Council enact, statute and ordain that in time comeing such as
shall neglect to enter in right of their wives during their lifetimes shall not upon
their offering to enter afterwards be entitled to any abatement of the ordinary dues
in use to be paid by unfreemen.” This arose from the case of Thomas Kyd, q.v.
11 Sept. 1745.—The Dean of Gild Council met for the last time before the
interruption caused by Prince Charles Edward’s capture of the city. David Nevey’s
is the last name entered as burgess and gild brother. The box was opened, and five
pounds stg. taken out and entrusted to the Dean of Gild. The court was constituted
anew by the Lords of Council and Session 6 Aug.

hundred and fourty-six years. The which day in obedience to ane act and warrand

nominating and appointing Thomas Allan, Dean of Gild, Hugh Hathorn, old Dean
of Gild, and George Gray, merchants, Samuel Neilson and Charles Mack, masons,
and James Herriot, wright, to exerce the power and office of Dean of Gild and
Councill for the purposes and to the effect therein mentioned.
            Sederunt—Thomas Allan, Dean of Gild.
            Hugh Hathorn, O.D.G.
            Samuel Neilson.
            Charles Mack.
            James Herriot.”

20 Aug. 1746.—The Dean of Gild Council duly met, but no burgesses were
admitted till 4 Jan. 1747.

1 Apr. 1747.—“The same day His Royal Highness William Augustus, Duke of
Cumberland, Brunswick, Lunenburgh, etc., etc., Captain General of all His’
Majestie’s land forces and Commander in Chief of the allyed army, etc., etc., etc.,
was by the Right Honble. George Drummond, Esq., Lord Provost of the City of
Edinburgh, Robert Montgomery, William Hamilton,
John Brown and Andrew Wardrop, baillies of the said city, Thomas Allan, Dean
of Gild, and the Gild Councill, and hereby is invested with the freedom of this city
as a testimony of their grateful sense of the glorious services done by his Royal
Highness to his Sacred Majesty and the British Nation in happily crushing the late
detestable Rebellion, giving a total overthrow to the rebells in the memorable
Battell of Culloden, restoring the publick tranquillity, makeing way for the free
exercise of goverment in this city, secureing the trade liberties and laws of Great
Britain, and transmitting to posterity along
with the immortal honours of a young hero the invaluable blessings enjoyed under
the auspicious reigns of the Protestant Princes of the illustrious House of
Hanover,— conform to an act of the Town Council of the date the 3rd day of
January last, 1747, and the seal of the city affixt.”

1 Apr. 1747.—“Act investing His Royal Highness William, Duke of Cumberland,
with the freedom of the city of Edinburgh.” (“The Butcher.”) (An ominous day !)

21 Mar. 1748. -The Town Council recommended to the Lord Provost to present
Mr. Thorntoun of Cattlehall with the freedom of the city, and to entertain him on
that occasion at the city’s expense.

1 July 1748.—Captains and others of the East India Company’s squadron, to be
admitted burgesses and gild brethren gratis. Marked E.I.C. in entries.

8 Nov. 1749.—(The Town Council) appointed the Dean of Gild and his Councill
to admitt and receav George Walker, Esquire, Commodore of the late squadron of
private ships of war called the Royall family, to be burges and gild brother of this
city in the most ample form.
(From Minutes of Town Council.)—11 July 1750.—“Anent the petition given in
by John M’Hardie, mert., lawfull son procreat betwixt the deceast John M’Hardie,
writer in Edinr., and Jean Jollie, his spouse, lawfull daur. to the decast John Jollie,
mert. burges of Edinbr., setting furth that the petitioner’s father haveing gone
abroad soon after his marriage in order to push his fortune was very suddenly
carried off by a feavor before he had any opportunity of returning home. That if
the petitioner’s farther had setled in this place he had a right by his wife to have
entered a burges, that the petitioner intending to carry on business as a mert. he
hop’t the council notwithstanding his father’s ommission would allow him to enter
in right of his grandfather and to authorise the Dean of Gild to admit him
accordingly, more especially as the petitioner by the mother’s side is descended of
a very ancient race of burgesses and has also a right.to enter by his wife as the
petition bears. Which haveing been read in Council the same was remitt to a
committee of their number and they to report. Accordingly this Day Baillie Robert
Baillie from the said committee reported ‘that they haveing considered the said
petition, and altho’ the petitioner’s father neglected or att least by his sudden death
was prevented from entering in right of his wife yett as the petitioner himself has
right to enter by his wife, lawfull daur. to Charles M’Hardie, mert. That therefor
the Dean of Gild and his Council should be ordered to admitt the petitioner a
burges and gild brother in right of his grandfather, by which no manner of loss is
sustained by the city as the fees of entering in both cases are the same as the report
under the hands of the Committee bears. Which haveing been considered by the
Magistrates and Councill they with the extra’ry deacons approved of the said
report and ordered the Dean of Gild and his Councill to admitt and receave the
petitioner to be burges and gild brother of this city in the right of John Jollie, mt.,
his grandfather, dispenseing with his father’s ommission. Whereanent ane extract
of these presents shall be a warrant.”

20 Nov. 1751.—“Mr. Sands, City Treasurer, represented that the indentures
entered into with James M’Crabie as ane apprentice with the city’s cassway layers
being now expired, and as the overseer of the city’s publick works informs that
M’Crabie is pretty much master of his business and that the toun will have
occasion for his service farther. That James Pirrie, son to James Pirrie, a souldier
in the garrison of Edinbr. Castle, was willing to enter into indentures on the like
termes with M’Crabie, whereforthe Treasurer desired the Council’s directions in
what is above represented. Which being considered they ordered the treasurer to
give M’Crabie a declaration with respect to his haveing faithfully served the city
during the years of his indentures upon M’Crabie’s acknowledging that he is fully
satisfied and paid of his wages. Also they agreed to continue M’Crabie in the
city’s service as a casswaylayer and to give him the ordinary wages during the
Councill’s pleasure. And they authorised the Treasurer to enter into indentures in
behalf of the city with the said James Pirrie on the like conditions with M’Crabie.”

7 Dec. 1751.—“Appointed the Dean of Gild and his Councill to admitt and
receave Dougall Young, weaver, to be burges of this city, dispensing with the dues
in consideration of his ingenuity in contriving a loom for weaveing herron nets,”
18 June 1755.—“Mr. David Flint, old Dean of Gild, represented he was well
informed that Richard Beckford, esquire, Member of Parliament for the City of
Bristol, had been generously pleased to signify that he was to give two hundred
pounds Jamaica currency annually for the four ensuing years in order to promote
the exportation of linnen made in Scotland from the Port of Leith. Therefore
moved the Councill that they would be pleased as a mark of their gratitude for this
singular favour to the country and to the City of Edinburgh in particular to order a
burges ticket, for Mr. Beckford, and to recommend to the city’s member when he
goes next to Parliament to deliver it himself with the Council’s best compliments.
Which having been considered by the Magistrates and Councill, they appointed
the Dean of Gild and his Councill to admit and receive the said Richard Beckford
a burges and gild brother of this city, dispensing with the Dues for the good
services done by him to the interest thereof. Whereanent these presents shall be a
warrant.”

18 July 1755.—Philip Yorke, Lord Royston (b. 30 Dec. 1722, d. 20 Jan. 1770),
afterwards 2nd Earl of Harwick, and (1770) Lord High Chancellor, was the eldest
son of Philip, ist Earl of Hardwick, by Margaret Cocks. The entry in the Burgess
Roll reads :—18 July 1755.—“ The which Day the Right Honble. George
Drummond, Esq., Lord Provost [of] the City of Edinburgh, James Stuart, Robert
Forrester, George Lind and John Learmonth, baillies of the said city, James Grant,
Dean of Gild, and the Gild Council, did and hereby do invest with the freedom of
this city Philip, Lord Roystoun, in testimony of their grateful sense of the many
eminent services done to Great Britain by The Right Honble. Philip, Earl of
Hardwick, Lord Chancellor, and his Lordship’s particular attention to the
improvement of this part of the United Kingdom, conform to an act of the Town
Council of this date.”
(The said act is much more concise.)
Among the “eminent services” were the Earl’s presiding at the trial of the Jacobite
peers after Culloden, in which capacity he must hear large responsibility for the
cruelly vengeful verdicts pronounced and executed. It was due to him that the act
was passed in 1748, for disarming the Highlands and making the wearing of the
kilt a criminal offence. The abolition of
” Hereditary Jurisdictions “ in 1746 must, however, be put to his credit.
Note.—2 Feb. 1757.—Gilson, Mr. Cornforth, B. and G., gratis, “for the eminent
services done by him to this city by improving the taste of the inhabitants in
church music.” He was appointed precentor of the new church 13 Mar. 1757, with
£5 above the other precentors, teaching them and the church music schools.

              SPECIAL TRADES [1761 - 1841].
These mark the first, or very early, appearance of certain names of trades. We find
such changes as “dyer” supplanting “litster,” “butcher” supplanting “flesher,” “tin-
plate-worker” for “white-iron smith.”

       ADDENDA TO ROLL OF EDINBURGH
                BURGESSES
          AND GUILD BRETHREN, 1701-1760.
Owing to the fact that occasionally the Town Council ordained that certain persons
be admitted burgesses and, guild brethren whose names were never entered on the
Register of the Dean of Guild and his Council, the following names do not appear
on the roll. -They were found in an “ Index of Council Burgesses, commencing
from the 1st day of October 1740 years,” and ending 10 September 1796. All “
gratis, by act of C.”

Editor’s note: The entries in the Addenda have been merged with the main body
of entries and can be identified by the color in the sample below.
Ward, Mr. Wm., of Staple Inn, London, attorney at law, B. and G. 7 Sept. 1757

          CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES [1761 - 1841].
See an act of the Town Council, Sept. 1759, upon a motion made by the then dean
of gild that there was two persons applying to be Burgesses in right of their wives.
That by an act of the Town Council 19 July 1583 it is enacted “that daurs. of
Burgesses shall lose the freedom if they are not reputed virgins. That this act had
been so applied that daurs. of B. could not communicate the freedom to a second
husband, which was the case of the two persons applying. Find & Declare that the
daurs. of a B. has right to communicate the freedom of the city to her second
husband in the event of her first husband not entering B. in her right.”

4 March 1761.—Robert Mitchell, p. to James Young, junior, barber, wigmaker
and hairdresser. This seems to be the earliest mention of this designation.

17 June 1761.—“Upon a Recommendation from the Governours of Herriots
Hospitall in favour of Robert Gilmore, Ropemaker in Bristo, Appoint the Dean of
Gild and his Council to admitt and receive him Burgess of this city gratis to this
effect only, Chat Peter Gilmore his son may have a title to be received into the
said Hospitall.”

11 Aug. 1762.—The five masters of the High School, Messrs. Alexr. Mathison,
John Gilchrist, Robert Farquhar, Alexr. Bartlet and James French, admitted B. and
G., gratis, for good services. “ Resolved that for the future none of the masters of
the High School shall be admitted Burgesses untill after they are five years in
office.” In 1763 an extraordinary number of cases occurred of a man’s being
admitted burgess on the same day that he had entered as apprentice for several
years. This suggests the explanation that they had not been booked at the time of
entering as apprentice, and did so, in a formal way, on the expiry of the
apprenticeship.

30 March 1763.—The Treasurer moved the Council to present with the freedom
of this city Sir William Baird of Saughtonhall, Baronet, and Captain James Hart
for the good services done by them to their King and Country during the late war;
both these gentlemen having also been particularly friendly to many of our
countrymen employed in his Majesty’s service in the East Indies. Which being
considered by the Magistrates and Council they appoint the Dean of Gild and his
Council to admitt and receive Sir William Baird of Saughtonhall, Baronet, as also
Captain James Hart, Burgesses and
Gildbrethren of this City for good services done to King and Country.

30 Nov. 1763.—“The Lord Provost represented that the military at present in the
Castle had been remarkably active in assisting the magistrates in quelling the late
mobs, and that it would be proper to give them some gratification for the great
fatigue and trouble they had in that matter. Which being considered by the
Magistrates and Council they with the extraordinary Deacons authorise and
appoint the City Treasurer to cause distribute a week’s pay among the private men.
Whereanent these presents shall be a warrant. And the Council also resolved to
compliment the officers of the said corps
with the freedom of the city for the assistance they gave the Magistrates upon that
occasion.”

15 Feb. 1764.—“It being represented by the Magistrates that it appeared by a
precognition taken before them that James Ireland, son to James Ireland, writer in
Edinburgh, had been guilty of breaking up the shop in the new Exchange
belonging to Robert Thomson, merchant, and thereafter had absconded. Upon
which they had advertised a Reward of Ten Guineas to be
paid by the City Treasurer to any person who should apprehend the said James
Ireland and upon his being convicted. The Council approved of the procedure of
the Magistrates in the said matter. It was at the same time represented that the
Magistrates had got information that the said James Ireland had made his escape to
Newcastle, whereupon the Lord Provost had wrote to the Lord Mayor of that place
desiring that he might take the trouble to cause search to be made there for him,
and that the Mayor of Newcastle had caused apprehend him after a pursuit of
fourty miles in which that gentleman had been at great pains as well as in many
other matters relating to the Interest of this City, and therefore it was moved that
the freedom of the city should be conferred on him for his good services and that
the Lord Provost should acquaint him thereof and at the same time desire of him to
pay the officer who apprehended Ireland in such manner as he should judge
reasonable, which afterwards would be repaid to him by the City Treasurer.”

19 Dec. 1764.—“It being represented by the Dean of Gild that an Index of
Honorary Burgesses would be very necessary and convenient and moved that the
same should be done and the Dean of Gild clerk authorised for that purpose, Did
therefore authorize Mr. Alves to make out the foresaid Index commencing from
Michaelmas one thousand seven hundered and fourty two and to be executed
betwixt and the first day of March next.”

7 Aug. 1765.—“Alexr. Newlands, mt, compearing, is made B. of this city in r. of
Alexr. Newlands, mt., B., his father, and he paid his dues, gave his oath, &c.
Thereafter it having been represented to the Dean of Guild and his Council that the
aforesaid Alexr. Newlands, mt., was only the natural son of Alexr. Newlands, mt.,
and consequently had no right, the Court Rescinds the above entry and Discharge
the Clerk of Court from giving out the Ticket.” [There is accordingly no entry on
the margin of dues paid.]

June 1766.—The Lord Provost signes James Stuart.

12 Nov. 1766.— Sir William Forbes, Barronet, compearing, is made Burges and
Gildbrother of this City as having served an apprenticeship to Messrs. Coutts
Brothers & Co., merchants, Burgesses & Gildbretheren thereof, and he paid the
usual fees of recording his Indentures and admission money & gave his oath, &c.
He was entered as apprentice, so, viz.:—

8 Oct. 1766.—Sir Wm. Forbes, Barronet, compearing is entered an apprentice to
Messrs. Couts Brothers & Co., merts., Burges & Gildbrethren for five years.

8 Apr. 1767.—Josiah Corthine, Esq., collector of H.M. Customs at Hull ; William
Hildyard, Esq., in Great Grimsby, Lincolnshire ; and Archd. Douglas at Exmouth,
Devonshire, admitted “burgesses and gildbrethren of this city in the most ample
form for the good services done by them to the Interest thereof by their humane
Conduct in saving a great property belonging to the citizens when the ship
‘Betsey’ was stranded on the Lincolnshire coast.”

13 May 1767.—“Considering that a practice has for some time prevail’d of giving
the freedom of the city to many persons indiscriminately which has been attended
with great Inconvenience, The Council Do therefore Enact & Declare that no
Burges Ticket shall be granted in time comeing to any person whomever, but such
as are invested with public character or shall have signalized himself in the service
of his countrey or this city.”

29 July 1767.—Letter from Mr. George Chalmers, inert, in Edinr., addressed to
the Lord Provost, stating that the present Postmaster-General, the Earl of
Hilsborough and Lord Despencer had agreed to order the mail to and from London
to pass by the direct course between Ferrybridge and Northallerton without
making the circuit of York, alteration to take effect on 10th Oct. next, which will
be four hours additional time to this city in their correspondence with London, and
which had been before solicited in vain from Postmasters-General. The Council
unanimously resolved to return this city’s thanks to
the present Postmasters-General, and to invest them with the freedom of the city,
and to send them copies thereof accordingly.

27 June 1769.—Robert Cock, skinner, was made B. as p. to David Murray,
skinner, B. He entered as p. 22 Aug. 1716, served his five years till 1721, and then
waited forty-eight years ere he was admitted B. 15 May 1770.—John Kellie, white-
iron smith and tinplate worker. This seems to be the first mention of tinplate.

guild officer, Represented That by mistake he had caused record a Burges above
mentioned by the name of Donald Ferguson mercht. Whereas his real name is
Donald Farquharson mercht., and the said Donald Farquharson being present
Craved that his Ticket might be made out Farquharson
which was his real name. The Court Appoint a Ticket to be made out to Donald
Farquharson merchant in place of Donald Ferguson mercht. And Declare
accordingly.
20 March 1771.—“John Thorburn, journeyman mason in Edinburgh compearing
is made Burges of this city Dispensing with the dues for good services done by
him to the interesfof this City by his distinguishing himself in a very remarkable
manner and acting with great intrepidity in assisting to extinguish the late fire in
the lawn mercate conform to an act of Council of date the thirteenth of February
last. Likeas the dean of gild & his Council in terms of said act Declare the said
John Thorburn his admission to be as valid effectual and sufficient to him as if he
had paid the whole fees in use to be paid by unfreemen and he gave his oath as use
is.”

23 Sept. 1772.—John Little, wright, B., as p. to James Brounhill, wright, B.

10 Feb. 1773.—“ Upon a petition from John Wood, merchant in Edinr. setting
furth that upon the twelfth day of April seventeen hundred and fifty-eight years, he
was admitted a Burges and Gildbrother of Edinburgh when he made faith and paid
the whole dues. That in recording his name in the gild court books he is called
James in place of John. Therefore Praying for an alteration of the record and that a
Ticket may be given out in the name of John Wood. The Dean of Gild and his
Council upon considering the said petition and examining witnesses on oath viva
voce in court as to the facts therein set furth Allow the record to be altered and a
Ticket to be given furth by the name of John Wood, and the record was
accordingly altered in presence of the Dean of Gild.”
Note.—There is no alteration in the volume, No. 13 of the Guild Register.

30 August 1775.—“Appoint the Dean of Gild and his Council to admit and
receive Burges and Gildbrother of this City in the most ample form Sir Grey
Cooper secretary to the right Honble. the Board of Treasury descended from the
ancient Family of Cooper of Gogar in this County whose ancestor Simon Cooper
appears upon Record to have been a great Baron in the year 1296— and whose
other ancestor Sir John Cooper the First Baronet of the Family represented the
County of Edinr. in the Scots Parliamt. for many years was one of the
Commissioners of the Kingdom at the Treaty of Rippon (sic) and in
other High Stations distinguished himself in the management of public affairs, in
consideration of the Family he represents and of his services to the Nation.”

23 Oct. 1776.—A petition was presented for James Whitit setting forth that on the
Eleventh of October last he was admitted a burges of the City In right of Elizabeth
Mairhead his wife the Daughter of a Freeman and paid the usual dues of
admission. That in Recording him in the Burges Book he is designed gardner in
Edinr. whereas his Proper designation is Wauker, and therefore praying the Dean
of Gild & Council would grant warrand for expeding his Burges Ticket as a
Wauker in place of a gardner. Which being considered by the Dean of Gild and his
Council They Granted warrant as Craved.

“ 10 September 1777.—The Dean of Gild and his Council Considering that this
book is much worn and some of the Leaves loose and that it is improper any more
Burgesses or Gildbrethren should be entered therein Appoint the loose leaves to be
fixed in the best manner and the book repaired Prohibite & Discharge the Clerk of
Court from entering any more Burgesses or Gildbrethren in this book & ordain a
new book to be got immediately.
CHARLES INNES, D.G.”

17 Dec. 1777.—Robert Clark, joiner. This seems to be the first mention of the
trade.

8 July 1778.—Thomas Dundas, Lieut-CoL, and Major James Gordon, both of the
Royal Edinr. Volunteers, admitted B. & G. gratis, and the other Major to be
admitted likewise as soon as he shall be named by his Majesty.

3 March 1779.— Bailie (Donald) Smith moved that as the Edinburgh Regiment is
now going abroad in the service of their country that the Magistrates may be
authorized to give the officers an Entertainment, of which motion the Council
approved and authorize accordingly.

9 Sept. 1779. — It was represented that James Camming, painter, was not a
Burges of this Burgh and as William Milne, painter, formerly his apprentice, has
procured a Burges Ticket and paid therefore, as deriving right thro the said James
Cumming. But upon searching the Record it really appealed That the said James
Cumming never was entered Burges himself consequently the said William Milne
could not be entered as a Burges apprentice. Therefore I John Grieve, Esqr., Dean
of Gild of the said City of Edinburgh Do hereby Declare That the said William
Milne is not a Burges of this Burgh, as set forth
in a sederunt of the Fifth of August last and I hereby Ordain the clerks and officer
to Return him his money.

7 Sept. 1780.—Wm. Miller, younger of Barskimming, B. and G., in the double
right of his fr. and his w.

21 March 1781.—£44 : 2s. to be paid to James Hewit, goldsmith, for making and
engraving gold box for holding Burgess ticket to be presented to Admiral Sir
George Bridges Rodney.

27 June 1781. — Hyde Parker, Esq., Vice-Admiral of the Blue Squadron of H.M.
Fleet, and the fifteen captains of H.M. ships presently stationed in Leith Roads,
were admitted Burgesses and Guildbrethren, gratis, by act of the Town Council, in
recognition of their eminent services; and an “entertainment” provided for them.

2 Jan. 1782.—The Lord Provost being about to go to London, the Council request
him to carry with him the Gold Box and Burgess Ticket for Admiral Rodney, and
to deliver it to him or to his family. Also to take the Burgess Tickets lately made
out for the captains of Admiral Barker’s Fleet not delivered here, and to deliver
them in like manner.

17 Jan. 1782.—43 burgesses were admitted, of these 31 were unfreemen, and two
were apprentices, booked apprentices, and admitted burgesses on the same day.

21 Feb. 1782.—M’Fell, Myles, vintner, admitted B., commonly called Lord
North. In Peter Williamson’s Directory, 1780-1, he is entered as “ M’Phell Miles,
vintner, commonly called Lord North, Jackson’s Close.”

17 July 1782.—Report by Dean of Guild, who had discovered many people with
no Burgess right, or trading on a licence in a line of business which did not entitle
them to that indulgence. He had published an advertisement in the newspapers,
and sent circular letters to offenders, in consequence whereof 132 had been
admitted burgesses and 76 burgesses and gildbrethren since Michaelmas 1781,
bringing in 972 stg. This year will bring in about 760.
Revenue for 10 years £262 :8 :6 annually. He proposes that the surplus be applied
for the building of a steeple for St. Andrew’s Church in George St. Remitted to
Lord Provost;s Committee for report.

31 July 1782.—“Robert Allan, first merchant Councilour moved that as John
Howard, Esquire, who has been at uncommon pains about the intended Bridewell
is to be in this City in a few weeks, he should be presented with the freedom of the
City. Which being Considered by the Magistrates and Council they did and hereby
do admit and receive the said John Howard, Esquire, of Cardington, as Burges and
Gildbrother of this City for the good services done by him as mentioned in the
foresaid motion.”

12 Nov. 1782.—Alexr. Cleugh had entered B. in r. of fr. some time ago, but same
not being sustained, he paid full fees. Now petitions repayment. Granted.
22 Oct. 1783.—Grant of twelve guineas to the Second Battalion of Lord
M’Leod’s Highlanders, as a testimony of the Council’s approbation of their
conduct in the late gallant defence of Gibralter.

12 Oct. 1785.—“The Council in testimony of their sense of the undaunted
Courage of Vincent Lunardi Esquire of Lucca in ascending with a Balloon and
passing the Forth to Fife, with the wind at south west at the manifest Risk of his
being blown into the German Ocean, admitted and received him a Burges &
Guildbrother of this City.”

6 Sept. 1786.—A piece of silver plate, to the value of thirty guineas voted to Wm.
Charles Little, Esq., of Libberton, on account of his polite and generous behaviour
relative to a free gift of the water on his grounds at Libberton, Bailie Gordon to
order the plate and deliver it. Mr. Little admitted Burgess and Guild Brother of the
City. In the autumn of 1786 a very large number were admitted burgesses, many
as unfreemen, with no claim for reduced “dues.” A considerable number also who
were admitted as having served an apprenticeship were entered at the same time as
entering upon their apprenticeship—the “booking “ having been omitted at the real
date of entrance. This seems to have been the result of a closer scrutiny into
qualifications for burgess-ship and exercise thereof. In Nov. 1786 131 names are
recorded.

20 Dec. 1786.—“Approved of Report of a Sub-Committee on a letter from John
M’Cliesh, Clerk to the Chamberlain, and authorised the City Chamberlain to make
payment to him of Sixty Guineas for making the Model of St. Andrew’s Church
with the intended steeple ; and Admitted and received the said John M’Cliesh a
Burges and Guildbrother of this City, dispensing with the dues for good services.”

M.T.C.—29 Aug. 1787.—“On motion from the Dean of Guild authorised him to
grant warrant to the City Chamberlain for repaying to Wm. M’Leod, gardner, the
fees paid by him at his admission as a Burges.”

22 June 1791.—“On the motion of the Lord Provost the Council admitted Colonel
Charles Graham of the forty-second Regiment of Foot, a Burges and Guilclbrother
of the city, and the Lord Provost was authorised to return the thanks of the Council
to him and the other officers of that Regiment for their attention in giving
immediate assistance with large parties at several dangerous fires which lately
happened, And authorized the Magistrates to give an entertainment to the officers,
and authorized the Lord Provost and Treasurer to give such a small duceur as they
may think proper to the Privates for their
good behaviour.”

29 March 1797.—Fletcher Yetts, Distributor of Water in the Castlehill Reservoir,
who had made a model (plan) last September of pipe track from Heriot’s

off the main cast iron distributor on the top of George Street with stop cocks, &c.,
admitted guild brother on motion of Bailie Coulter, gratis, for this good service.
